## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{100}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why does a tool call that parses cleanly still need a runtime between it and the world?_

Calling an external tool transforms an isolated language model from an advisory text generator into an active distributed system participant capable of mutating persistent real-world state. Because a stochastic model can invent invalid parameters, target incorrect filesystem paths, or hallucinate task completion, generating a tool call cannot grant the authority to execute it. The runtime must enforce a hard structural boundary between model proposal and tool execution: inspecting argument schemas, verifying caller permissions, and isolating side effects within sandboxed execution environments. Furthermore, because tool responses become context observations, partial failures and network timeouts must be reported faithfully rather than masked by invented outcomes. Managing tool calling establishes the core invariant of agent engineering: authority remains strictly with the deterministic runtime, while the model functions solely as a proposal engine.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Trace a proposed tool call through validation, authorization, dispatch, and a correlated observation into the next model call
- Design a tool descriptor that separates structural validation from action-time preconditions enforced with the effect
- Distinguish tool discovery and connectivity from the grants required to invoke an operation
- Select blind retry, endpoint deduplication, or reconciliation for an uncertain effect from operation semantics and loss rates
- Design bounded observations that preserve execution status, omission information, and the scope of available evidence
- Compare waiting and resumption strategies for long-running tools by detection delay, inference cost, and retained supervision
- Evaluate toolkit granularity by context cost, cost per accepted task, and enforced reach across structured, general-purpose, and computer-use interfaces

:::
## The Tool Boundary {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-boundary}

An agent asked to restart a container on a staging server emits a short tool call. The host runtime checks the call against the tool's schema, confirms that this session may restart that container, and sends `POST /containers/srv-stage-04/restart`. Two seconds later the socket times out. The request may be lost, delayed, still executing, or completed without a delivered reply. A retry could restart healthy workers, and the first attempt can still take effect after the timeout.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_a.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with only the Authority axis lit in purple; Horizon and State axes gray."}

*The Authority axis, closed at the tool boundary by mediating every proposed call.*
:::

Nothing about this failure is exotic. The repair agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) meets the same questions on every turn of the connection-pool repair. It reads `src/pool.py`, replaces text derived from the version it read, runs the test suite, and receives a log far longer than the next model call can hold. Each step is a tool call, and each can be rejected, left running, completed without a reply, or answered with more output than the model should see.

The pieces built so far do not settle these questions. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract gave the model a structured way to propose a call, and the memory chapters already relied on tools to read sources, search indexes, and update records without examining what happens between a proposal and its result. A retrieval result identifies the version it observed, but keeping that version current until a later edit is an action-time precondition that something must enforce. A proposal names an operation and its arguments. It does not decide whether this task may run the operation, whether an earlier attempt already ran it, or what the next model call should receive.

This chapter builds the runtime's tool boundary, the path between a proposed call and the environment it would change. The boundary validates each proposal, checks it against the task's grants, dispatches it, tracks what is known about its effect, and returns a bounded observation matched to the call. Throughout, it keeps apart the three things the timeout blurs, the distinction from @sec-vol3-intro between what the model proposed, what effect the operation had, and what evidence the runtime holds about either.

The sections follow one call and then widen. @Sec-vol3-tool-calling-unix-analogy lays out the mediated round trip and the protection requirement that organizes it. @Sec-vol3-tool-calling-schemas types the request and couples action-time checks to the effect, and @sec-vol3-tool-calling-mcp separates discovering a tool from being allowed to use it. @Sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency decides when an uncertain effect may be retried. @Sec-vol3-tool-calling-streaming and @sec-vol3-tool-calling-observation-parsing bound what returns to the model without losing what it means. @Sec-vol3-tool-calling-async extends the contract to jobs that outlive a model turn, and @sec-vol3-tool-calling-toolkit-design and @sec-vol3-tool-calling-visual-actuation use those mechanics to evaluate tool catalogs and computer-use interfaces.

## Tool Subsystem Architecture {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-unix-analogy}

@Lst-vol3-tool-call-turn shows the staging restart as one turn of the loop, in a provider-neutral form. The runtime reports what it knows about this attempt, and the next model call receives that result together with the earlier request and proposal.

::: {#lst-vol3-tool-call-turn lst-cap="**One turn of the tool-call loop**: A call identifier correlates the proposed call with its result. The next model call receives the timeout as an unknown effect, not as evidence that the restart did not happen."}
```json
[
  {"role": "user",
   "content": "Stage-04 is serving a stale config. Restart it."},
  {"role": "assistant",
   "content": [
     {"type": "tool_call", "id": "call_1", "name": "restart_container",
      "arguments": {"container_id": "srv-stage-04"}}]},
  {"role": "tool",
   "content": [
     {"type": "tool_result", "call_id": "call_1",
      "content": {"transport_status": "timeout", "effect_status": "unknown"}}]}
]
```
:::

The runtime correlates each result with its corresponding call using an explicit identifier rather than message order alone. That identifier establishes message lineage across asynchronous turns, but correlation alone does not resolve whether the target service completed the requested mutation. Preventing duplicate restarts requires an operational contract for idempotency, developed in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency. Even if the subsequent model turn assumes that the service recovered, the runtime preserves the underlying uncertainty, authorizing a retry only when supported by fresh environment evidence or an enforced idempotency guarantee.

### One mediated round trip {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-round-trip}

@Sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract established the model-side call surface\index{Call surface}, where an inference engine emits structured invocation blocks rather than unstructured natural text. Once the model outputs a proposal, the runtime assumes full custody of execution. Between the moment a tool call leaves the model and the moment an observation enters the context of the next turn, the runtime mediates the entire round trip across the four coordinated stages in @fig-vol3-tool-call-loop: argument validation screens inputs against tool schemas, policy authorization verifies security grants, dispatch executes the permitted operation while tracking outcomes, and observation shaping normalizes raw results into bounded prompt payloads.

Request validation parses proposed arguments against the tool's declared schema, verifying required fields, data types, value ranges, and relational invariants among parameters. Dynamic constraints that depend on volatile environment state cannot be settled at this boundary; the system must evaluate them at the execution boundary rather than inferring them from historical context. Next, operation authorization verifies the active session's security grants against the targeted resource, evaluating concurrency budgets, rate limits, and access policies for read operations as well as state mutations.

Following authorization, dispatch submits the permitted operation to the underlying execution provider while outcome tracking maintains execution identity and status. This tracking distinguishes cleanly among pre-dispatch rejections, active background tasks, successfully reported results, and unconfirmed execution states. A transport timeout simply indicates that the runtime exceeded its waiting deadline, leaving the remote execution state unconfirmed. Finally, observation shaping maps the raw return value back to the originating call identifier, truncating payloads to fit context budgets, sanitizing terminal escape sequences, and tagging the output with accurate status metadata. If log output must be truncated, the payload explicitly discloses the omission; if a system returns an asynchronous job ticket, observation shaping reports it as an acknowledgment rather than a completed effect.

These stages refine the general turn lifecycle introduced in @sec-vol3-intro-execution-lifecycle. Certain validation checks must execute at the remote endpoint because safety requires atomicity with the state change itself; for example, an edit conditioned on a source version requires the version check to occur in lockstep with the update. Consequently, the host runtime and the remote endpoint each enforce their respective boundaries. The endpoint checks access independently, even for requests that the host runtime already cleared. This division reflects the end-to-end argument applied to system protection: an authorization check that depends on private endpoint state can be finalized only at that endpoint, making preliminary host-level checks useful performance optimizations rather than authoritative substitutes [@saltzer1984endtoend].

::: {#fig-vol3-tool-call-loop fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The tool-call loop**: Validation and authorization can reject a proposed call before dispatch. For a dispatched call, the runtime tracks the available outcome and shapes the return into a bounded observation matched to its call identifier. An unknown effect remains unknown in that observation." fig-alt="Flow diagram showing model tool calls passing through runtime validation, authorization, dispatch and outcome tracking, and observation shaping before the next model call. Rejected calls return structured errors without reaching the environment."}
![](images/svg/tool_call_loop.svg)
:::

When the serving interface returns native structured call blocks, the runtime extracts the proposed operation and arguments directly. When a model emits proposals within unstructured free text, the runtime must first detect and parse those fragments before validation can proceed. Constrained decoding eliminates syntactic parsing failures by enforcing grammar rules directly during token generation (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-grammar-constrained). Yet syntax alone never establishes operational safety: whether the target resource exists, whether the observed version remains current, and whether the current session holds execution privileges remain runtime checks that no decoding grammar can verify.

### Complete mediation {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-complete-mediation}

Securing the tool interface rests on a foundational tenet of computer protection design: complete mediation [@saltzer1975]. At the tool boundary, mediation must govern both reads and mutations. Emitting a tool name does not grant the model ambient runtime authority, nor does receiving an observation make external data trusted.

::: {#dfn-complete-mediation .callout-definition title="Complete mediation"}

***Complete mediation***\index{Complete mediation!definition}\index{Tool actuation!complete mediation} requires every proposed access to pass through an enforced authorization boundary before it reaches the protected resource. In an agent runtime, the return path is also mediated so that observations enter context under explicit access, payload, and status contracts.

1. **Significance**: A valid-looking call cannot bypass the checks governing what the session may read, change, or disclose.
2. **Distinction**: Schema validation establishes structural admissibility, not permission. Observation normalization establishes a usable representation, not the truth of its contents or immunity to prompt injection, attacker-controlled content that attempts to redirect the model (@sec-vol3-security).
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating a prompt instruction such as “never delete production data” as an access barrier. The runtime must enforce the restriction even when the model proposes the prohibited action.

:::

Anderson formalized the architectural component required to enforce complete mediation: the reference monitor [@anderson1972computer].

::: {#dfn-reference-monitor .callout-definition title="Reference monitor"}

***Reference monitor***\index{Reference monitor!definition}\index{Tool actuation!reference monitor} is the enforcement component through which every access to a protected resource passes. It must be tamper-proof, always invoked, and small enough to verify. In an agent runtime, the host's validation and authorization path is the reference monitor for proposed tool calls, and each endpoint's access check is a second monitor for the resources that endpoint owns.

1. **Significance**: The three requirements turn complete mediation from an intention into a checkable property of the runtime's structure.
2. **Distinction**: The policy specifies permitted accesses, whereas the reference monitor provides the non-bypassable mechanism that evaluates and enforces those rules on every attempt.
3. **Common pitfall**: Adding a tool route that does not pass through the monitor, such as an unrestricted shell with network access beside a checked file adapter, which makes the adapter's checks advisory.

:::

These three requirements dictate concrete architectural choices at the tool boundary. *Tamper-proofing* ensures that neither generated model tokens nor untrusted data ingested from external systems can alter the authorization rules enforced by the runtime. *Always-invoked* mandates that every operational path pass through the monitor without exception. Exposing an unrestricted shell runner alongside a sandboxed file tool, for example, completely undermines the protection boundary, because the agent can bypass file restrictions by issuing shell commands. Finally, *verifiability* requires policy decisions to be deterministic, auditable software checks. Although an auxiliary classifier or guardrail model can score operational risk, probabilistic inference cannot be verified in the strict systems sense; the monitor itself must enforce deterministic access boundaries.

Two operational rules follow directly from complete mediation, and this chapter applies them systematically. The *grant rule*\index{Grant!grant rule} establishes that execution authority derives solely from the session's active security grants, re-evaluated on every invocation. Read operations demand the same rigorous mediation as state mutations, because returning private records discloses sensitive data even when environment state remains unchanged. A syntactically valid schema, an enforced tool choice, an advertised description, a staged descriptor, or a known handle never enlarges those grants. The *evidence-scope rule* establishes that an observation confirms only the specific metric or condition measured by the tool during that invocation. Reporting that an operating system process exited with code zero confirms only process termination; it does not prove overall task completion, which remains a distinct judgment governed by invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}). Furthermore, raw output text remains untrusted data even after the runtime strips terminal formatting and normalizes metadata; observations supply empirical evidence of state, but they carry no ambient authority to dictate subsequent actions.

### Batches and forced calls {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-batches-forced-calls}

A single model response can propose multiple tool calls simultaneously, such as reading three source files in parallel. When operations are strictly read-only and independent, the runtime can dispatch them concurrently, correlating each returned observation with its respective call identifier. A failure in one read does not invalidate concurrent operations that succeeded. Nevertheless, every invocation in the batch must individually pass validation and authorization, and the combined batch consumes from a shared resource and rate-limit budget.

State mutations complicate concurrent execution. For example, reading `src/pool.py` concurrently with another call that edits it yields non-deterministic results depending on scheduling race conditions. When tools declare a trustworthy **resource footprint**\index{Resource footprint!definition}—the explicit set of state each call reads and writes—the runtime can evaluate potential data hazards. If neither operation writes to state read or written by the other, the pair satisfies Bernstein's conditions for noninterference and permits safe concurrent dispatch [@bernstein1966]. However, this guarantee relies entirely on the completeness of footprint declarations; any hidden side effect or undeclared shared dependency invalidates the concurrency guarantee.

Operations with opaque side effects, such as arbitrary shell commands, possess unknown footprints. In such cases, the runtime must either isolate the execution environment, serialize calls conservatively, or reject batched execution in favor of fine-grained tools. Furthermore, when operations exhibit causal dependencies, those ordering constraints must originate from the workflow policy or an explicit dependency graph; the sequential order of tokens generated by the model does not constitute reliable evidence of intended execution order. Nor does batching imply atomicity: a batch forms a transaction only when the underlying tool substrate explicitly provides transactional all-or-nothing rollback semantics.

The runtime can also govern whether the model proposes an action. Using serving-level **tool-choice control**\index{Tool-choice control!definition}, the runtime can configure tool calling as optional, mandate that the model invoke at least one tool, restrict selection to a specific named operation, or forbid tool execution altogether. Orchestration engines use these constraints to guide execution phases—for instance, forcing a diagnostic read before permitting an edit, or disallowing tool calls to force a final textual summary. Crucially, tool-choice controls merely shape model generation; under the grant rule, forcing a tool choice confers no operational authorization.

Executing each stage of this mediated round trip requires an unambiguous request representation, establishing a strict operational boundary between static schema validation and dynamic preconditions verified at dispatch time.

## Tool Interface Schemas {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-schemas}

Recall the connection-pool repair (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) right at the transition from revision `r17` to `r18`. The model has inspected `src/pool.py` and emitted a proposed patch. Before applying that modification to real infrastructure, the host runtime must resolve four fundamental questions: Which tool operation did the model select? What do its arguments denote? Does the current task possess the authority required to execute the mutation? And crucially, does the underlying target file still match the exact source state on which the model based its proposal? A well-formed JSON payload satisfies syntactic structure, but syntax alone cannot answer these operational questions.

A **tool descriptor**\index{Tool descriptor!definition} defines an operation's functional purpose, input parameters, expected return values, and execution side effects. Within that descriptor, the **argument schema**\index{Argument schema!definition} codifies machine-checkable constraints: required fields, primitive types, permitted enumerations, and supported size bounds. These specifications serve two distinct audiences: natural-language descriptions guide the language model in selecting and parameterizing tools, while the surrounding runtime and downstream service endpoints validate and enforce the interface contract.

### Descriptor semantics {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-descriptor-semantics}

To make these guarantees concrete, consider a tool named `conditional_replace_file`. This tool replaces a single file in the task's designated workspace, but commits the change only if that file still matches the expected source version. The descriptor must establish several semantic invariants: `path` resolves strictly relative to the designated workspace rather than an arbitrary host location; `expected_version` identifies the baseline source revision the model inspected; and `replacement` supplies the complete replacement content encoded in the endpoint's documented format. Under this specification, passing an empty replacement string explicitly truncates the file to zero bytes instead of serving as a shorthand instruction to leave contents unmodified.

Full file replacement keeps this precondition example transparent, though production runtimes often prefer line-anchored patches or structured diffs to minimize token generation overhead. As detailed in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-interface-design, structured diffs reduce generated output while demanding identical coordination between precondition verification and atomic mutation.

@Lst-vol3-tool-schema illustrates the machine-checkable argument structure. Notice that the request payload contains neither a credential token nor a privilege flag through which the model might expand its access rights. The host runtime independently binds the invocation to the task's authorized execution context.

::: {#lst-vol3-tool-schema lst-cap="**Conditional file replacement arguments**: The schema describes the request's structure. Its descriptions do not implement path confinement, authorization, or atomic version checking."}
```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["path", "expected_version", "replacement"],
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "path": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1,
      "description": "File path relative to the designated workspace."
    },
    "expected_version": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1,
      "description": "Source version returned with the inspected file."
    },
    "replacement": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Complete replacement text, written as UTF-8."
    }
  }
}
```
:::

The descriptor's result contract requires equal precision. A completed replacement reports the affected path and its newly assigned revision token. A version conflict explicitly reports that the target diverged and the replacement was not applied. Furthermore, the runtime must clearly distinguish deterministic client errors—such as malformed arguments or insufficient authority—from indeterminate transport failures where the endpoint's state remains unknown after a dropped connection. A comprehensive descriptor explicitly models all four outcomes, including network timeouts where no acknowledgment arrives.

Precise field names and descriptions eliminate avoidable ambiguity during generation. For example, a file-reading tool should state whether its offset argument counts bytes, characters, or lines. Similarly, a timeout parameter must state its measurement units and specify whether it bounds connection establishment, remote execution, or end-to-end response delivery. While clear documentation guides the model toward valid parameters, the execution runtime must programmatically enforce all defaults, enumeration sets, and numerical bounds. Grounding model generation in explicit tool documentation yields measurable reliability improvements: @patil2023gorilla demonstrated that models trained to condition tool invocations on retrieved API documentation invent nonexistent operations and hallucinate invalid arguments far less frequently than models relying solely on unconditioned prompting.

### Structure, permission, and state checks {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-boundary-checks}

When processing a tool call, the runtime first verifies that the model produced a fully completed candidate, adhering to the invocation contract defined in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract. If generation halted prematurely due to token limits or client disconnection, the runtime aborts immediately; a partial payload that happens to form syntactically valid JSON cannot be trusted as an intentional tool request. Once execution status confirms a complete output, the runtime parses the candidate and validates its arguments against the tool's registered JSON schema before performing any domain checks.

In our replacement example, omitting `expected_version` or supplying a numeric `path` fails structural validation immediately. Setting `"additionalProperties": false` in @lst-vol3-tool-schema likewise causes the parser to reject hallucinated arguments such as `force` or `recursive`. However, structural conformance resolves only syntax. Verifying whether the path resides within the task's assigned sandbox, and determining whether the target still contains the inspected source revision, require distinct evaluation steps. As summarized in @tbl-vol3-schema-contract, the runtime enforces these guarantees across layered boundaries.

| Check                | Question for the proposed edit                                                                   | What passing does not establish                                                        |
|:---------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Argument structure   | Are the required fields present with the declared types and supported constraints?               | The path is permitted, the version is current, or the replacement is a correct repair. |
| Domain preconditions | Does the target support this operation, and does its version match when the update takes effect? | The session has authority to modify it.                                                |
| Authority            | Do the task's current grants permit this operation on the resolved target?                       | The arguments fit resource limits or the operation will succeed.                       |
| Resource limits      | Does the request fit enforced payload, execution, and result limits?                             | The returned evidence will establish task acceptance.                                  |

: **Checks at the tool boundary**: Each check establishes a different part of the action contract. Source-dependent checks must remain valid through the operation they protect. {#tbl-vol3-schema-contract tbl-colwidths="[18,41,41]"}

A string formatted as a file path does not constitute a confined resource reference.[^fn-toctou-path-tools] The tool implementation must canonicalize and resolve the target inside the authorized workspace, accounting for symlinks, directory traversal escapes, and path alias changes that could redirect the operation. Similarly, declaring `replacement` as a string does not bound its encoded memory footprint. Production adapters enforce explicit byte-size limits on incoming payloads, bound the volume of captured diagnostic output, and apply strict execution timeouts. Static schema validation handles input syntax, whereas dynamic state verification, path confinement, and resource throttling remain runtime obligations. @Sec-vol3-app-b-json-schema supplies a bounded edit descriptor along with an operational schema-review checklist covering required fields, buffer limits, explicit units, and variant semantics.

[^fn-toctou-path-tools]: **Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use**: Bishop and Dilger analyzed the UNIX file-access race in which the binding of a name to an object changes between a program's check and its later use, so a privileged program can be steered onto a file it never checked [@bishop1996checking]. A tool adapter that validates `src/pool.py` and then reopens the path by name inherits the same window: a symbolic link swapped in between turns a permitted edit into an edit elsewhere. Resolving the path once and operating on the resolved object, rather than re-resolving the string, is what closes it. \index{TOCTOU!tool path confinement}

Grammar-guided decoding effectively eliminates syntactic errors during generation, as demonstrated in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-grammar-constrained. However, token-level grammar masks cannot resolve filesystem references, evaluate access-control policies, or verify concurrent version tags. The host runtime must validate the materialized tool request, while the downstream endpoint verifies dynamic preconditions during physical execution. This separation instantiates the typed action contract (principle \ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi})\index{Principle!typed action contract}, securing the boundary between generative text output and physical system actuation.

### Conditional updates {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-conditional-updates}

The `expected_version` parameter binds the read contract of @sec-vol3-persistent-governance directly to the mutation contract enforced here. An earlier read operation confirmed only that `src/pool.py` matched revision `r17` at the specific instant of observation; that read did not lock or reserve the file for future modification. If a concurrent process or another agent alters `src/pool.py` before the edit request arrives, applying a patch derived from `r17` would silently overwrite those intervening modifications, causing a classic lost-update anomaly.

To guarantee serializability, the storage service must verify the expected version and commit the replacement as a single atomic **conditional update**\index{Conditional update!definition}—the storage equivalent of a hardware compare-and-swap (CAS) primitive.[^fn-optimistic-validation-tools] In this example, the workspace source service executes the entire sequence inside a single coordination boundary: it resolves the target file, verifies that its current revision matches `expected_version`, writes the new content, and publishes the resulting revision token. Decomposing this sequence into non-atomic operations—such as reading the revision, verifying it in user space, and then issuing a write—reopens a race window where concurrent writers can intervene. The atomic conditional update closes this time-of-check to time-of-use gap.

[^fn-optimistic-validation-tools]: **Optimistic Concurrency Control**: Kung and Robinson proposed letting transactions read without locks and validating, at commit, that nothing they read had changed, restarting any transaction that fails validation [@kung1981optimistic]. The expected-version check is that validation for a single file, and it inherits the same economics: a conflict is cheap when writers rarely collide, but under contention each failed validation costs the agent a fresh read and a new proposal, which is paid in model turns rather than in microseconds. \index{Optimistic concurrency control!conditional update}

This execution branch yields two distinct operational outcomes:

1. If the current source revision remains `r17`, the update commits the replacement and returns `r18`, identifying the new revision produced by the edit.
2. If another writer modified the source first, the version check fails. The service rejects the replacement, leaves the storage state unaltered, and returns an explicit version-conflict status.
Following a conflict, the runtime directs the agent to perform an authorized read of the updated source file and synthesize a fresh proposal, rather than blindly overwriting the intervening modifications.

This concurrency guarantee holds only as long as all mutations route through the shared coordination boundary. If external processes or unmanaged scripts modify files directly on disk, bypassing the version service, version tokens offer no protection and the endpoint cannot ensure integrity. Dry-run previews follow the identical principle. A dry run confirms that a proposed patch applies cleanly against revision `r17` at the moment of evaluation, but it establishes no lock on that revision. The runtime must re-verify all preconditions, permissions, and version tokens when executing the live write.

Receiving a successful `r18` confirmation verifies that the file modification committed to disk, but it does not establish that the underlying connection-pool bug has been resolved. Demonstrating functional correctness requires empirical validation: a subsequent passing run of `test_waiter_notified_on_return` provides concrete evidence that the patch resolves the targeted race condition, while broader task acceptance continues to follow the project's verification suite. At the network layer, a dropped reply leaves the caller uncertain whether the server committed the edit or failed before processing the payload. The retry and idempotency contracts analyzed in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency resolve this operational uncertainty.

### Rejection diagnostics {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-rejection-diagnostics}

When an operation fails, the runtime must return a structured, bounded diagnostic that isolates the failure condition without leaking information beyond the task's authorized grants. For example, a structural rejection should identify the missing `expected_version` property, and a concurrency conflict should state that revision `r17` has been superseded. Conversely, permission rejections must refuse access cleanly without exposing directory structures, environment variables, or path hints that an agent might probe. The runtime logs whether a rejection originated locally during client-side schema validation or remotely at the service endpoint, allowing downstream decision logic to distinguish between an unattempted proposal and a failed remote mutation. Clear, bounded diagnostics provide the model with the exact evidence needed to synthesize a valid revision, which must then traverse the same validation pipeline.

Every tool descriptor exposed to an agent consumes context window capacity. Deciding which descriptors to stage dynamically, and balancing expressive specialized tools against minimal generic primitives, forms the toolkit-design challenge addressed in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-toolkit-design. Before an agent can select or execute tools, however, the runtime requires a standardized transport protocol to discover, bind, and communicate with external service interfaces.

## Interoperable Tool Discovery {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-mcp}

In practice, a tool implementation such as `conditional_replace_file` can live in several environments: an in-process adapter compiled into the application, a standalone background daemon, or a remote microservice managed by another team. Before the model can propose a valid call, the host runtime must determine which operations that endpoint exposes and how to encode their arguments. This discovery phase supplies that interface metadata. Under the grant rule, however, learning that an operation exists confers no authority to execute it: discovery defines interface syntax, whereas authorization governs execution rights.

### The Model Context Protocol {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-mcp-protocol}

When building a self-contained agent with a small, static set of tools, registering local functions directly in-process is simple and fast. But when multiple host applications must connect to independently maintained tool services, custom point-to-point integration quickly becomes impractical. The underlying challenge is combinatorial. Without a shared interface, $N_{\text{host}}$ host runtimes integrating $N_{\text{tool}}$ tool services require up to $N_{\text{host}} \times N_{\text{tool}}$ bespoke adapters. Standardizing on a common protocol reduces this burden to $N_{\text{host}} + N_{\text{tool}}$ implementations, allowing each side to build to the specification once.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/tool_calling_margin_adapter_count.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two small graphs. Left: three host boxes each wired to four tool-service boxes, twelve crossing adapter lines, labeled N host times N tool. Right: the same hosts and services each wired once to a central protocol box, labeled N host plus N tool."}

*A shared protocol turns pairwise adapters into one implementation per side.*
:::

Decoupling tools across a protocol boundary also introduces critical fault isolation. When a tool runs in a separate process, a memory leak, segmentation fault, or unhandled blocking call crashes only the tool server rather than tearing down the primary agent orchestration loop. Even so, protocol standardization does not eliminate engineering responsibilities: integrators must still define tool semantics, audit version compatibility, and enforce security policies. Local in-process plugins and out-of-process tool servers represent deliberate deployment trade-offs rather than mutually exclusive or evolutionary stages.

The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**\index{MCP!definition}\index{Model Context Protocol|see{MCP}} exemplifies this architecture. MCP structures integrations across three distinct entities: a host application (such as an interactive environment or agent runtime), clients that manage connections, and servers that expose capabilities. Servers can run as local child processes or as remote network services. This architectural division clarifies integration responsibilities rather than prescribing a specific execution sandbox [@mcp2025specification].

Each deployment model matches different operational demands. A local child process keeps filesystem operations adjacent to the working copy and simplifies process lifecycle management. Conversely, a remote service can centralize credential storage, connection pooling, and backend access without replicating sensitive configurations across every host machine. Yet both options introduce distinct failure modes and resource boundaries: an unconfined local process still reaches whatever local filesystem it is granted, while a severed network link can leave an in-flight operation executing invisibly on a remote server. Architects must choose deployments based on where resource governance and policy enforcement belong, evaluating transport latency relative to tool execution duration rather than presuming any transport topology is universally superior.

### Tool listing and invocation {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-listing-invocation}

MCP defines two primary wire operations for tool interaction: `tools/list` to discover available tool definitions and `tools/call` for execution.[^fn-jsonrpc-correlation-ids] Each definition advertises a unique name, a natural-language description, and a JSON Schema governing accepted arguments; an invocation names the target tool and supplies a matching argument dictionary. These messages establish the mechanics of interface exchange rather than a task's execution rights. The MCP tools specification [@mcp2025specification] defines these message formats and explicitly mandates server-side input validation and access controls.

[^fn-jsonrpc-correlation-ids]: **JSON-RPC Request Identifiers**: MCP frames these messages as JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, each carrying an `id` that its response echoes [@mcp2025specification]. That identifier does the work of this chapter's call identifier, matching a reply to its request on one connection. It says nothing about whether a second `tools/call` with the same arguments is the same intended effect, which is why retry safety needs the separate operation identity developed in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency. \index{JSON-RPC!request identifier}

To trace where policy boundaries sit during execution, consider a repository server advertising two illustrative operations: `read_source` and `apply_patch`. A concrete integration sequence proceeds through several verification checkpoints:

1. The host's client queries `tools/list` and binds each accepted schema explicitly to that server instance and its locally governed tool policy. Explicit binding ensures that an identically named tool advertised by another server cannot silently shadow or replace the expected implementation.
2. The host determines which accepted definitions to expose in the model context for the connection-pool repair task.
3. When the model proposes an operation, the host runtime validates the arguments against the schema and verifies task-level authorization before transmitting the request.
4. Upon receiving `tools/call`, the endpoint independently verifies the request against the underlying operating system permissions and data access controls it manages.

For the connection-pool repair, discovering that `apply_patch` exists leaves the permitted edit paths and the expected-version preconditions unchanged. The guarantee of atomic, conditional updates derives entirely from the server implementation, never from an encouraging function name. If an endpoint fails to provide conditional-update guarantees, the runtime must reject it as incompatible with the task's safety contract.

### Discovery and authority {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-discovery-authority}

Tool descriptions provided during discovery are untrusted external inputs. A description might accurately summarize an operation, omit critical failure modes, or embed prompt instructions that attempt to steer model behavior. Even an authenticated server can supply a misleading description, because verifying a server's identity does not imply endorsing every claim it emits. A host runtime must never promote claims such as “approved for all workspaces” into an authorization grant.

Filtering which tools appear in the model prompt narrows the attack surface, but catalog filtering alone cannot replace per-call enforcement. Task grants evolve dynamically, and call arguments select specific resources at runtime. Authorizing an agent to inspect `src/pool.py` does not permit it to read unrelated credentials or transmit private source code to an external service. Furthermore, defense-in-depth requires the server or backing service to enforce its own perimeter rather than assuming every client performs flawless checks. Host authorization and endpoint authorization protect different assets and operational domains; neither supersedes the other. On the return path, protocol framing cleanly differentiates a tool result payload from a system message, but framing does not disarm adversarial text within the payload—an attack vector examined thoroughly in @sec-vol3-security.

A documented security vulnerability demonstrates the systemic danger when ambient credential reach serves as the sole barrier between discovery and side effects.

::: {#ws-07-github-mcp-2025 .callout-war-story title="GitHub MCP private-repository leak (2025)"}

**Context**: In May 2025, Invariant Labs demonstrated an attack on an agent connected to GitHub through its MCP integration [@milanta2025github]. The user owned both a public and a private repository and directed the agent, running in a desktop client, to inspect open issues in the public repository. The agent's GitHub access token held permissions that spanned both repositories.

**Mechanism**: An attacker filed an issue in the public repository containing prompt instructions designed to redirect the model. After reading the issue as an ordinary tool result, the agent executed the server's schema-valid tools to inspect the user's private repositories and then opened a pull request in the public repository containing the exfiltrated contents. Every tool call remained within the personal access token's broad credential scope, and no runtime check verified whether the target repository matched the task's intended scope. Although the client prompted users to confirm tool calls by default, developers frequently enable an "Always Allow" setting to avoid operational friction.

**Impact**: The public pull request disclosed sensitive information, including the private repository name, relocation plans, and salary details. Invariant Labs characterized the breakdown as an architectural failure in agent runtime mediation rather than a software defect in GitHub's server implementation.

**Fix**: The researchers recommended enforcing context-aware access control at runtime—such as restricting an agent session strictly to the target repository identified by the user—alongside continuous monitoring of agent-server traffic. They also observed that model alignment training alone failed to stop the attack.

**Systems lesson**: Discovery, schema validity, and credential authentication all succeeded. The failure was an absence of complete mediation (definition \ref{dfn-complete-mediation}) against the task's explicit grants, which should have blocked the initial private-repository read—a read-only $A_0$ action—well before any write operation occurred.

:::

This exploit succeeded because three distinct conditions coincided:

1. The agent ingested untrusted external text that mounted an indirect prompt injection [@greshake2023not].
2. The agent held ambient authority broader than its active task required.
3. The runtime provided tools capable of public mutations.

Eliminating any single condition breaks the attack chain. The second condition represents a classic systems security failure: the *confused deputy* problem [@hardy1988confused]. A confused deputy is an authorized program tricked into misusing its authority on behalf of an unprivileged party because the system fails to tie the authority exercised to the party directing the action. In this incident, the agent exercised the user's repository credentials on behalf of the remote attacker who authored the issue text. While @sec-vol3-security analyzes defenses against prompt injection and unauthorized exfiltration channels, the tool runtime boundary directly governs the second condition. The runtime neutralizes confused deputy attacks by evaluating every tool call against the task's explicit grants rather than delegating authority to ambient credentials.

::: {#chk-07-complete-mediation .callout-checkpoint title="Discovery is not permission"}

A repository server advertises a schema-valid `apply_patch` tool whose description says “use any path needed to complete the repair.” The current task permits edits only to its designated working copy. Later, a read result includes a request to upload repository contents to an external endpoint.

- [ ] **Discovery vs. permission**: Which information does discovery supply, and which claimed permissions must the host refuse to derive from the description?
- [ ] **Per-call checks**: Why must an allowed tool still be checked against the proposed arguments and current grants at dispatch? What must the endpoint enforce independently?
- [ ] **Read authority**: Why does the read operation require authorization even though it does not edit a file?
- [ ] **Returned text**: What do bounded serialization and provenance labels establish about the returned text, and what do they leave open about its influence on the model?
- [ ] **Placing the check**: In war story \ref{ws-07-github-mcp-2025}, at which call would a per-call check against the task's grants have refused, and which of the three enabling conditions would that remove?

:::

Discovery establishes how to address an operation, and authorization determines whether a given task may attempt it. Yet neither mechanism resolves whether an in-flight mutation actually took effect when a network connection drops or a response times out. Because permission to initiate an action does not confer permission to blindly repeat it when the outcome is uncertain, robust execution requires explicit operation identity and idempotency guarantees.

## Retrying Uncertain Actions {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency}

Consider the staging-container restart introduced earlier. When `POST /containers/srv-stage-04/restart` times out, the client cannot distinguish between several fundamentally different physical realities: the request may have been dropped in transit, delayed in a network queue, or accepted by the daemon. The restart process might still be running, might have partially reconfigured the service before halting, or might have completed successfully while only the acknowledgment was lost. A client-side timeout[^fn-rpc-call-semantics] records only that the caller stopped waiting for a response; it conveys no information about endpoint execution state [@cristian1991understanding].

Deciding what to do next requires understanding two orthogonal properties: the operation's repeat behavior and empirical evidence about the earlier attempt. Prompting the language model to retry answers neither question.

[^fn-rpc-call-semantics]: **Remote Call Semantics**: Birrell and Nelson's foundational remote procedure call package stated its guarantee with precision: if a call returned, the remote procedure had executed exactly once; if an exception was reported, it had executed either once or not at all, and the caller received no indication of which had occurred [@birrell1984rpc]. A timed-out tool call inherits this second case directly. An agent runtime must preserve "once or not at all" as an explicit, unsettled status rather than collapsing it into a conventional failure that invites an immediate retry. \index{Remote procedure call!failure semantics}

::: {#dfn-uncertain-outcome .callout-definition title="Uncertain outcome"}

***Uncertain outcome***\index{Uncertain outcome!definition}\index{Settlement!uncertain outcome} is the recorded status of a dispatched operation whose effect the runtime can neither confirm nor exclude, because its reply was lost, late, or never produced. The operation stays unsettled until an endpoint deduplication contract, a reconciliation query, or an authorized decision establishes what happened.

1. **Significance**: An unsettled mutation blocks any retry that could duplicate it. Under blind retry, the duplicate rate tracks the reply-loss rate almost one for one (notebook \ref{nbk-07-settlement-budget}).
2. **Distinction**: A definite failure provides actionable knowledge, whereas an uncertain outcome represents missing information. A network timeout creates an epistemic void rather than a failed execution.
3. **Common pitfall**: Recording a timed-out restart as a definitive failure, which improperly authorizes the very retry that duplicates the mutation.

:::

### Delayed attempts {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-delayed-attempts}

A probe that reads an unchanged service state provides valuable evidence about the present, yet it cannot guarantee that a delayed request will not execute in the near future. Suppose the runtime dispatches restart attempt A, but the network buffers or delays the packet in transit. When the client-side timeout fires, the runtime queries the container state and correctly observes that the container has not restarted. If the runtime treats this unchanged state as definitive proof of nonexecution, it dispatches attempt B, which arrives promptly and completes the restart. Moments later, the delayed attempt A finally reaches the service and restarts the container a second time.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/tool_calling_margin_delayed_attempt.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Timeline with a runtime lane and a service lane. Attempt A leaves the runtime as a long dashed arrow. The runtime times out, probes the service, and hears unchanged. Attempt B then arrives and causes restart 1; the delayed attempt A lands afterward and causes restart 2, labeled second restart."}

*An unchanged probe cannot rule out an attempt still in flight.*
:::

The probe returned completely accurate telemetry, but the runtime drew a flawed inference: it mistook "not yet observed" for "cannot still happen." An attempt already executing inside the service produces an identical hazard. Sending an asynchronous cancellation request settles this ambiguity only if the endpoint explicitly confirms what halted and whether any side effects committed or could still commit. Safe repetition therefore demands much more than a client timeout followed by an optimistic read.

### Idempotent actions {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotent-actions}

Deciding whether to retry an unacknowledged tool call depends on the physical consequence of running the operation a second time.

::: {#dfn-idempotent-action .callout-definition title="Idempotent action"}

***Idempotent action***\index{Idempotent action!definition}\index{Idempotency!definition} is an operation whose repeated application has the same effect on a specified state as one application, $f(f(s)) = f(s)$, under the operation's stated conditions.

1. **Significance**: Idempotence is the cheapest settlement. A timed-out idempotent call can be retried without reconciliation, which removes the duplicate-effect path priced in notebook \ref{nbk-07-settlement-budget}.
2. **Distinction**: The property belongs strictly to the implemented operation and its target state; it does not guarantee identical network responses, zero resource consumption, or isolation from concurrent writes by other processes.
3. **Common pitfall**: Assuming idempotence from an HTTP verb or tool name alone. Operations such as restarting a service or appending a log entry introduce new state transitions on every invocation, regardless of the API naming convention.

:::

Setting a configuration field to a desired value can be idempotent[^fn-idempotent-peirce-tools] with respect to that field. Incrementing a counter, appending a record, or restarting a service usually describes an additional event on each execution. The endpoint's implementation determines which semantics the tool actually provides, and @tbl-vol3-tool-idempotency sorts the three semantics by what a repeat means and what the runtime must still check before allowing one.

[^fn-idempotent-peirce-tools]: **Idempotent** (Latin *idem*, "the same," and *potent*, "power"): Benjamin Peirce introduced the term in his 1870 survey of linear associative algebras to describe an element that remains unchanged when raised to any positive integer power, $x^n = x$ [@peirce1881linear]. Systems engineering adapts this mathematical formulation to system state: executing an idempotent mutation multiple times leaves the system in the exact state as executing it once. Crucially, algebraic idempotence guarantees nothing about identical return payloads, execution costs, or hidden side effects introduced along the execution path. \index{Idempotency!etymology}

| Operation semantics               | What repetition means                                    | What the runtime must still consider                                                           |
|:----------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Read without an intended mutation | Obtain another observation, possibly of a changed source | Access and disclosure permission, resource cost, and the version the result describes          |
| Set a desired state               | Reapply a value that may already hold                    | Intervening writes, conditional-update rules, and any additional effects the endpoint performs |
| Produce another event             | Append, charge, restart, or otherwise add an effect      | A deduplication contract or sufficient evidence that another execution is safe                 |

: **Repeat behavior at the tool boundary**: Safety follows the implemented operation and its conditions, not a universal classification of tool names. {#tbl-vol3-tool-idempotency tbl-colwidths="[25,33,42]"}

The conditional-update scenario in @tbl-vol3-tool-idempotency illustrates this subtlety. Suppose a repair tool predicates its patch on source version `r17`. Once it installs `r18`, repeating the conditional request cannot accidentally overwrite subsequent edits, provided the endpoint checks the version and applies the write atomically. The repeated request returns an optimistic concurrency conflict rather than a success status. While this atomic check protects the repository from corruption, it leaves open the question of whether the earlier attempt or a competing process committed `r18`. Resolving that attribution requires tracking operation identity across attempts through an endpoint result-recovery contract.

Repeat behavior operates along an orthogonal axis from the authority levels $A_0$ through $A_3$ defined in @sec-vol3-intro-hsa. An authority level governs whether an agent may execute an action autonomously; repeat behavior dictates whether the runtime can safely re-execute that action after an ambiguous failure. These concerns intersect directly at level $A_2$, which @sec-vol3-intro-hsa reserves for external operations backed by bounded automatic retries or well-defined compensating actions. An external tool call qualifies for $A_2$ autonomy only if the runtime settles every transport timeout prior to retrying, relying on verified idempotent semantics, an endpoint deduplication contract, or bounded reconciliation.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-tool-calling-settlement
#| echo: false
# RETRY LOSS PATH: hypothetical probabilities, not measured failure rates.
# LOAD: Independent request/reply loss; delivered requests execute successfully.
# EXECUTE: One original attempt, with exactly one retry after any timeout.
# GUARD: Distinguish a lost original reply from a delivered duplicate request.
# OUTPUT: Display probabilities under this deliberately limited model.
from mlsysim import *

class SettlementBudget:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical independent message-loss probabilities.
    request_loss = 0.02
    reply_loss = 0.02
    workers = 50  # hypothetical fleet size
    calls_per_worker_day = 4_000  # hypothetical mutating calls per worker per day

    # 2. EXECUTE: enumerate the timeout and duplicate-effect paths.
    timeout_probability = 1 - (1 - request_loss) * (1 - reply_loss)
    duplicate_probability = (1 - request_loss) * reply_loss * (1 - request_loss)
    calls_per_day = workers * calls_per_worker_day
    duplicates_per_day = calls_per_day * duplicate_probability

    # 3. GUARD: independently checked path probabilities.
    check(abs(timeout_probability - 0.0396) < 1e-12, "Timeout loss paths")
    check(abs(duplicate_probability - 0.019208) < 1e-12, "Duplicate needs delivered retry")
    check(calls_per_day == 200_000, "Fleet call volume")
    check(abs(duplicates_per_day - 3841.6) < 1e-6, "Rare per call, routine per day")
    check(request_loss == reply_loss, "Prose states one loss rate for both directions")

    # 4. OUTPUT: display assumptions and results through unit-aware formatters.
    loss_str = fmt_percent(request_loss, style="prose", precision=0)
    timeout_str = fmt_percent(timeout_probability, style="prose", precision=2)
    duplicate_str = fmt_percent(duplicate_probability, style="prose", precision=4)
    workers_str = fmt_int(workers)
    calls_per_worker_day_str = fmt_int(calls_per_worker_day)
    calls_per_day_str = fmt_int(calls_per_day)
    duplicates_per_day_str = fmt_int(round(duplicates_per_day))
    _q = fmt(request_loss, precision=2, commas=False)
    _r = fmt(reply_loss, precision=2, commas=False)
    timeout_math = fmt_math(rf"1-(1-{_q})(1-{_r})")
    duplicate_math = fmt_math(rf"\Pr(\text{{duplicate effect}}) = (1-{_q})\times {_r}\times(1-{_q})")
```

::: {#nbk-07-settlement-budget .callout-notebook title="Which retry path duplicates an effect?"}

**Problem**: Suppose inbound requests and outbound replies each experience an independent `{python} SettlementBudget.loss_str` probability of packet loss. Every delivered request executes successfully, and every caller timeout triggers exactly one blind retry of a non-idempotent operation without deduplication. Dropped packets are assumed to be permanently lost rather than delayed. What is the probability that a single dispatched action executes more than once, and how many duplicate mutations will an agent fleet induce each day?

**Math**: The initial attempt times out whenever the outbound request or the returning reply is lost, occurring with probability `{python} SettlementBudget.timeout_math`, or `{python} SettlementBudget.timeout_str`. Producing an unintended duplicate mutation requires a specific sequence: the original request must reach the endpoint, its confirmation reply must be lost in transit, and the subsequent retry request must successfully reach the endpoint:

`{python} SettlementBudget.duplicate_math`

This evaluates to `{python} SettlementBudget.duplicate_str`; whether the retry's own confirmation reaches the caller has no bearing on whether the endpoint mutated twice. In a fleet of `{python} SettlementBudget.workers_str` workers where each worker executes `{python} SettlementBudget.calls_per_worker_day_str` mutating calls per day, the system processes `{python} SettlementBudget.calls_per_day_str` daily calls. Under this naive retry policy, the fleet triggers approximately `{python} SettlementBudget.duplicates_per_day_str` duplicate mutations every single day.

**Systems insight**: The duplicate execution rate tracks the reply-loss rate almost one-to-one because creating a duplicate requires losing a reply between two successfully delivered requests. Losing an initial request produces only an unexecuted, harmless timeout. While halving reply loss reduces duplicate mutations by half, implementing an endpoint deduplication contract eliminates this failure mode entirely. At production scale, protocol-level deduplication contracts—not network hardening—serve as the primary reliability control. Note that this simplified model ignores delayed packets, which introduce additional duplicate execution paths.

:::

### Operation identity and endpoint contracts {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-operation-ids}

A **logical operation ID**\index{Operation ID!definition}, commonly called an idempotency key\index{Idempotency key|see{Operation ID}} in transactional storage and payment systems, identifies a single intended effect across multiple transport attempts. As Pat Helland observed, any distributed messaging substrate that survives network partitions and process crashes must occasionally retransmit packets; consequently, the receiving endpoint, rather than the transport network, must assume responsibility for rendering duplicate messages harmless [@helland2012idempotence]. An **attempt ID**\index{Attempt ID!definition}, in contrast, tracks an individual request-response exchange over the wire. When the agent runtime retries an unacknowledged restart, it preserves the original operation ID while generating a fresh attempt ID for transport tracing. Conversely, if an agent later issues a distinct, deliberate request to restart the same container, the runtime must allocate a brand-new operation ID, even if the target arguments are identical. Deriving operation IDs purely from argument hashes conflates distinct operational intents, whereas generating a new identifier after every timeout destroys deduplication entirely.

An operation identifier provides safety only when governed by an explicit endpoint contract. This contract binds the operation ID to the caller's identity, the target resource scope, and the serialized payload. If a client reuses an active operation ID with mismatched arguments, the endpoint must reject the request with a client error (such as an HTTP 409 Conflict) rather than silently dispatching a mutated operation. Furthermore, the endpoint must enforce access control independently on each attempt: possessing a valid operation token does not substitute for authorized credentials when dispatching actions or retrieving retained execution results.

The contract must also govern concurrent and interleaved requests. If a duplicate request arrives while the original attempt is actively executing, the endpoint should return an in-progress or pending status instead of spawning a parallel worker. If a duplicate arrives after execution finishes, the endpoint returns the previously computed and retained result. To uphold this guarantee under crash failures, the endpoint's persistence mechanism must atomically link the side effect with its stored completion record. If a worker applies the mutation and crashes before persisting the result, a simple log of request receipt cannot prove that re-execution is safe. Where the underlying resource supports it, enclosing both the mutation and the result record within a single database transaction guarantees atomic state transitions. When acting against external services lacking transactional boundaries, the endpoint must coordinate with the downstream system's native deduplication mechanisms. @Fig-vol3-idempotency-flow diagrams this stateful deduplication flow: the runtime creates a unique operation ID once and carries it across retry attempts, while the service endpoint queries its deduplication store to triage requests into four operational paths (reserving execution for fresh IDs, returning cached results for completed IDs, signaling backoff for in-progress operations, or rejecting mismatched payloads as ID conflicts).

::: {#fig-vol3-idempotency-flow fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**One operation, many attempts**: The runtime creates the operation ID once and gives each attempt a fresh attempt ID, so a timeout leads either to another attempt of the same intent or, once attempts run out, to an unresolved outcome. The endpoint's lookup, scoped to caller and resource within its retention window, decides whether a request returns a retained result, a pending status, or an ID conflict, or executes. Only the last branch applies the effect. Recording the result inside the same transaction boundary, where the effect permits one, keeps a crash from leaving an applied effect without the record that deduplicates its retries." fig-alt="Two-part flow diagram. On the left, a runtime column: admit the intent and create the operation ID once, then attempt k with the same operation ID and a fresh attempt ID, then timeout or lost reply looping back to the attempt, then attempts exhausted with an unresolved outcome. A request arrow goes to an endpoint lookup of the operation ID, and a dashed reply arrow returns. The lookup fans out to four branches: found and completed returns the retained result; found and still running returns a pending status; found with a different payload is rejected as an ID conflict; not found applies the effect and records the result inside one dashed transaction boundary."}
![](images/svg/idempotency_nonce_execution_flow.svg)
:::

@Lst-vol3-dispatch-operation-id illustrates the client runtime's implementation of this protocol. The runtime assigns the operation ID once upon admitting the intended mutation, then generates a fresh attempt ID for every network transmission. If repeated retries exhaust the attempt budget, the function returns an explicit unresolved outcome rather than propagating an uncaught exception. This design ensures that transport uncertainty surfaces directly to downstream reconciliation logic rather than disappearing into an unhandled error path. Because this retry loop is safe only when the remote endpoint guarantees deduplication, the runtime invokes this path exclusively for tools whose descriptors formally declare compliance with the operation ID contract.

::: {#lst-vol3-dispatch-operation-id lst-cap="**Retrying one intended effect**: The operation ID stays fixed across attempts, and exhausting the attempts yields an unresolved outcome. The loop is safe only against an endpoint that deduplicates by operation ID within its retention window."}
```python
def dispatch_mutation(transport, tool, args, op_id, max_attempts=3):
    # op_id was created once, when the runtime admitted this intent.
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            reply = transport.post(tool, args,
                                   operation_id=op_id,
                                   attempt_id=new_attempt_id(),
                                   timeout_s=transport.timeout_s)
        except (TimeoutError, ConnectionError):
            backoff(attempt)
            continue                     # same op_id; endpoint deduplicates
        if reply.status == "id_conflict":  # op_id reused with other args
            return {"op_id": op_id, "outcome": "rejected"}
        return {"op_id": op_id, "outcome": reply.status,  # completed or
                "result": reply.result}                   # pending
    return {"op_id": op_id, "outcome": "unresolved"}    # reconcile next
```
:::

Enforcing safety at the effect boundary is equally essential when managing superseded or zombie workers. Distributed schedulers commonly coordinate task assignment through leases—time-bounded claims on granted authority [@gray1989leases]. If a worker encounters an unobserved execution stall (such as a lengthy garbage collection pause or network blip), its lease may expire. The orchestrator reassigns the task to a second worker while the first worker remains active, creating a split-brain scenario where both workers execute mutations concurrently. Sizing lease durations well above the 99th percentile of observed execution latency reduces the frequency of overlapping executions, but statistical padding cannot eliminate the failure mode entirely. True mutual exclusion requires fencing at the destination resource, such as associating every task reassignment with a monotonically increasing epoch number that the destination endpoint verifies on every write before committing state changes.[^fn-epoch-sequencer-tools]

[^fn-epoch-sequencer-tools]: **Epoch Checks at the Resource**: Distributed lock services encountered this exact failure mode when stale lock holders continued mutating storage after their leases lapsed. The Chubby lock service addressed this with a sequencer: an opaque token containing the lock name, mode, and generation number, which clients transmit alongside mutating requests and target servers validate before committing writes [@burrows2006chubby]. The critical architectural insight is location: because a zombie worker cannot detect its own staleness, the mutating resource itself must enforce fencing by rejecting out-of-order epoch numbers. \index{Fencing token!epoch number}

A deduplication contract is incomplete without an explicit retention window. Endpoints must publish how long they retain operation IDs and cached results, as well as how they handle delayed requests that arrive after that retention boundary has elapsed. Once the retention window expires, resubmitting an old operation ID risks being treated as a brand-new request, reintroducing duplicate-execution risks. An idempotency token guarantees exactly-once execution semantics only when paired with active endpoint deduplication, durable coupling between side effects and result records, and an unambiguous retention schedule. While @sec-vol3-durable-execution examines durable logging and state recovery in depth, the tool runtime must never assume stronger guarantees than the underlying interface explicitly provides.

### Reconciliation {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-reconciliation}

When an endpoint lacks native deduplication support, the runtime must attempt to settle ambiguous operations through **reconciliation**\index{Reconciliation!definition}: an authorized, bounded inspection of external system state. Obtaining an operation-specific receipt (such as an execution log entry or transaction identifier bearing the caller's unique metadata) yields vastly stronger evidence than merely observing that the target system currently matches the desired state. A concurrent agent or human operator might have independently produced that state, or an earlier successful mutation might have already been overwritten by a subsequent update. Runtime diagnostics must maintain this epistemic distinction cleanly, rather than synthesizing a false success receipt for an unverified call.

Reconciliation works reliably only when designed prior to dispatch. A mutating tool operating over an endpoint without deduplication can be formalized as a three-part interface:

$$\mathbb{T}_\theta = \langle \text{actuate}(\theta),\ \text{probe}(\theta, s_0),\ \text{compensate}(\theta) \rangle$$ {#eq-vol3-legacy-tool-contract}

In @eq-vol3-legacy-tool-contract, $\text{actuate}(\theta)$ performs the desired mutation $\theta$. The verification probe $\text{probe}(\theta, s_0)$ is an authorized read operation, authored alongside the tool, that evaluates whether the intended postcondition holds relative to an initial baseline state $s_0$ captured immediately before dispatch. The optional compensation routine $\text{compensate}(\theta)$ provides an authorized procedure for mitigating partial or unintended side effects if execution falters.[^fn-saga-compensation-tools] Crucially, the probe must be implemented ahead of time as part of the tool contract: allowing an agent model to improvise verification queries on the fly after a timeout replaces transport uncertainty with unverified heuristic guesswork. Capturing the baseline state $s_0$ before dispatch provides the essential reference point. For example, before appending a configuration block to a remote file, the adapter records the file's initial length and cryptographic hash; after a timeout, the probe can decisively distinguish among three distinct states—appended exactly once, completely unchanged, or altered concurrently by an external actor—which a naive post-hoc file read cannot discern.

[^fn-saga-compensation-tools]: **Compensating Transactions**: Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem introduced sagas for long-lived business processes that cannot hold database locks across their entire duration: the workflow executes as a sequence of discrete transactions, where each forward step is paired with a compensating action that semantically neutralizes its effects if a subsequent step fails [@garciamolina1987sagas]. A compensating transaction executes as an entirely new forward action rather than an in-place database rollback; processing a payment refund, for instance, leaves both the original charge and the subsequent credit in the ledger. For this reason, tool architectures must treat compensation as a separate authorized operation requiring its own execution budget and outcome settlement, rather than pretending the initial mutation never occurred. \index{Saga!compensation}

Observing an "unchanged" probe result justifies an immediate retry only when backed by definitive structural guarantees. The runtime must either verify that the original attempt can no longer execute (for example, because its connection dropped and server-side socket teardown guarantees non-delivery), or rely on inherently idempotent semantics where repeat execution is harmless. Without those assurances, the delayed-attempt hazard illustrated in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-delayed-attempts remains fully active. Furthermore, reconciliation probes are themselves distributed network calls that can time out, fail, or exceed their allotted latency budgets, leaving the state unresolved.

Under these conditions, the only sound engineering decision is to classify the action as an unsettled outcome. The runtime preserves the operation identity alongside all gathered telemetry, suppresses automated retries, and escalates the ambiguity to an administrative reconciliation pipeline or human operator. A partially applied mutation frequently requires specialized remediation; many real-world actions lack mathematical inverses, and compensation remains an independent mutation with its own potential failure modes. Downstream tasks that depend strictly on the uncertain operation must block until settlement completes, whereas independent parallel subtasks can safely continue executing. Regardless of whether the final state is settled as completed, pending, or permanently ambiguous, the runtime must format these operational diagnostics concisely so that subsequent agent reasoning cycles can adapt without hallucinating state.

## Observation Stream Truncation {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-streaming}

An automated repair agent running a test suite may encounter a process that terminates with a definitive exit code while generating a log far too vast to fit within the subsequent model request. Conversely, a remote network operation may time out with an uncertain execution state while its local connection layer still captures valuable diagnostic telemetry. Determining the concrete execution outcome of a tool invocation and deciding what subset of telemetry to stage into the prompt are distinct systems responsibilities. An agent runtime must maintain this architectural separation rather than collapsing nuanced execution states into an opaque success or failure string.

Tool execution telemetry encounters two distinct resource boundaries on its return path. **Capture**\index{Observation capture!definition} governs the physical resources—kernel memory, disk storage, CPU cycles, and wall-clock time—spent receiving output from an external process or service. Context staging (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging) governs the logical volume of tokens admitted into the model's prompt after filtering, normalization, and serialization. A brief shell command such as `grep -rn` or an unconstrained compiler build can emit hundreds of megabytes in seconds. Without rigorous capture limits, the runtime risks buffer overruns, pipe deadlocks, or host memory exhaustion long before prompt construction begins.

### Bounded output capture {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-bounded-capture}

An execution adapter requires a bounded mechanism to consume child process output as it is generated. Waiting for a child process to exit before draining its output streams invites catastrophic failure: operating system pipe buffers have fixed capacities (often 64 KB on modern Linux kernels). When a child fills its standard output buffer, its write calls block until the reading process drains the pipe. Conversely, blindly buffering output into memory leaves the host exposed to an unbounded producer. The runtime implementation must continuously service its communication channels while strictly enforcing capture limits through bounded in-memory buffers and quota-managed disk storage.

The canonical failure mode in tool execution is a **pipe deadlock**\index{Pipe deadlock!definition}, which establishes a circular wait[^fn-circular-wait-deadlock] across two bounded pipes. An adapter communicating with a child process over standard input and standard output manages two unidirectional kernel pipes. Suppose the host writes a large payload to the child's input pipe and defers reading standard output until writing completes. If the child process emits verbose startup diagnostics before consuming its input, the output pipe fills, causing the child's write call to block. Concurrently, the host fills the input pipe buffer, causing its own write call to block.
