Both processes sleep interruptibly while waiting for the other to read, halting forward progress until an external watchdog timer terminates the task. Resolving this requires structural decoupling: the adapter must set all file descriptors to non-blocking mode and multiplex reads and writes across an asynchronous event loop, or dedicate concurrent worker threads to drain standard output and standard error independently. Draining output streams must never block on transmitting input.

[^fn-circular-wait-deadlock]: **Circular Wait**: Coffman, Elphick, and Shoshani identified four conditions that must all hold for a deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and a circular chain of processes each waiting on the next [@coffman1971]. Two full pipes satisfy all four, since each side holds its own buffer, cannot take the other's, and waits on it. A readiness loop removes the circular wait, because the host never blocks on one channel while the other has bytes to move. \index{Deadlock!circular wait}

An operational capture policy must also define explicit behavior when limits are reached. When incoming data exceeds a retention threshold, the runtime can either drop subsequent bytes while continuing to drain the pipe to prevent process stalls, or actively terminate the executing process. The runtime must persist telemetry recording which policy was triggered and whether byte loss occurred. Because continuously reading and discarding gigabytes of runaway output still burns CPU cycles and context-switch overhead, an output-volume limit complements execution timeouts and kernel resource controls (such as POSIX process quotas or cgroup limits) rather than replacing them. Process termination is itself an asynchronous state transition with its own failure semantics, addressed alongside cancellation mechanisms in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-governance.

Within these capture boundaries, the runtime extracts the most informative evidence for model evaluation. For software engineering and compilation workloads, preserving an initial prefix and a trailing suffix captures the critical context: build systems print environment configuration, command invocations, and compilation flags at the start, while emitting panic stack traces, assertion failures, and summary verdicts at the very end. However, intermediate warnings or early test failures can easily be lost in the omitted middle. A production capture policy must therefore disclose the exact magnitude of its omissions, while specialized diagnostic filters can selectively extract recognized error patterns from the middle stream.

@Lst-vol3-head-truncation illustrates why naive head-only truncation fails in automated workflows. In this representative test log, the panic trace and assertion failure appear only after tens of thousands of passing test cases.

::: {#lst-vol3-head-truncation lst-cap="**Where head-only truncation cuts**: The invocation context sits at the top of the log and the failure sits at the bottom. A policy that keeps only the first bytes returns the banner and passing tests and discards the panic."}
```text
$ cargo test --all
   Compiling core v0.1.0 (/workspace/core)
running 48219 tests
test engine::scheduler::test_fifo ... ok
[... 48,217 further passing tests ...]
test memory::paging::test_allocator ... FAILED
---- memory::paging::test_allocator stdout ----
thread 'test_allocator' panicked at src/memory.rs:142:9:
assertion `left == right` failed
test result: FAILED. 48218 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored
```
:::

Under a head-only policy, the model receives a nonzero exit status with zero explanatory context, forcing it to guess at root causes rather than making informed repairs. A **head-and-tail policy**\index{Head-and-tail truncation!definition} resolves this by partitioning the observation byte budget $M_{\text{obs},\max}$ across three components:

$$M_{\text{obs},\max} = M_{\text{head}} + M_{\text{notice}} + M_{\text{tail}}$$ {#eq-vol3-observation-byte-budget}

In @eq-vol3-observation-byte-budget, $M_{\text{head}}$ reserves space for the initial execution prefix, $M_{\text{notice}}$ allocates bytes for an explicit truncation disclaimer, and $M_{\text{tail}}$ preserves the most recent output suffix. The adapter implements this with fixed memory overhead: $M_{\text{head}}$ bytes are captured into a linear buffer until full, after which incoming bytes increment an omission counter while feeding a ring buffer of size $M_{\text{tail}}$ that continuously overwrites its oldest contents. When the child process exits, the adapter serializes the head buffer, an omission notice detailing the exact count of dropped bytes, and the ring buffer in chronological order. @Fig-vol3-stream-ingestion diagrams this bounded buffering pipeline: as stdout and stderr stream from child process pipes, the adapter captures initial diagnostic lines into a fixed head buffer, routes intermediate overflow into an unread count counter, and retains terminal lines in a circular tail buffer, composing an explicit truncation envelope that discloses omitted byte volume and exit status.

::: {#fig-vol3-stream-ingestion fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Bounded capture before staging**: The adapter drains each bounded pipe from one readiness loop, so neither channel stalls the child, and enforces a byte limit and a deadline on capture. The head fills once, the tail ring overwrites its oldest bytes, and the middle is counted but not kept, so capture memory stays fixed however long the process writes. The staged observation carries status, head, a notice of the measured omission, and tail within the byte budget $M_{\text{obs},\max}$; a retained record, when authorized, lets later calls read omitted ranges by handle." fig-alt="Left-to-right datapath with five stages. A child process writes stdout and stderr into two bounded pipes in an adapter, which feed a readiness loop annotated with a capture limit in bytes and an execution deadline. Capture buffers hold a head that fills once, a dashed omitted middle whose bytes are counted, and a tail ring that overwrites its oldest bytes. A staged observation stacks process and capture status, head, a notice of bytes omitted, tail, and an inspection handle, under the equation M obs,max equals M head plus M notice plus M tail. An arrow leads to the next model call, where the payload is measured in tokens. A dashed optional path stores a retained record with quota, expiry, and access checks, which serves bounded range reads to the inspection handle."}
![](images/svg/vol3-stream-ingestion.svg)
:::

Line counts provide presentation convenience but offer no memory safety guarantees, because an individual line can span arbitrary gigabytes. Systems runtimes must enforce byte limits strictly across all capture and parser buffers. Ingestion layers must handle character encoding boundaries and multi-byte decoding errors explicitly, truncating on valid Unicode code points before calculating token lengths. Ultimately, the model context is billed and constrained in tokens, not bytes. The token budget must account for schema framing, invocation provenance, exit status fields, and truncation notices. Staging an observation must leave sufficient headroom for task history, system prompts, and model generation tokens; tool observations must never monopolize the total context window.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-tool-calling-observation-budget
#| echo: false
# What: Price a bounded observation retained in a specified set of later calls.
# How: Separate an illustrative byte/token estimate from serialized payload size.
from mlsysim.core.units import MB, Mtoken, USD, byte, token
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_math, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_usd

class ObservationBudget:
    # LOAD: Hypothetical corpus, serialization, selection, and billing assumptions.
    raw_bytes = 24 * MB
    bytes_per_token = 3 * byte / token
    window_tokens = 128_000 * token
    shaped_tokens = 4_000 * token
    remaining_turns = 30
    input_price = 3 * USD / Mtoken
    cached_fraction_price = 0.10

    # EXECUTE: Only the shaped payload is eligible for the priced later requests.
    raw_tokens = (raw_bytes / bytes_per_token).to(token)
    raw_windows = (raw_tokens / window_tokens).to_base_units().magnitude
    shaped_share = (shaped_tokens / window_tokens).to_base_units().magnitude
    carried_tokens = shaped_tokens * remaining_turns
    carried_cost_uncached = (carried_tokens * input_price).to(USD)
    carried_cost_cached = carried_cost_uncached * cached_fraction_price

    # GUARD: Check the illustrative magnitudes without claiming task adequacy.
    check(raw_tokens.magnitude == 8_000_000, "raw token estimate")
    check(raw_windows == 62.5, "raw log exceeds whole window")
    check(carried_tokens.to(token).magnitude == 120_000, "selected later input")
    check(abs(carried_cost_uncached.magnitude - 0.36) < 1e-12, "uncached cost")
    check(abs(carried_cost_cached.magnitude - 0.036) < 1e-12, "cached cost")

    # OUTPUT: Derived prose numbers use shared formatters.
    raw_size_str = fmt_memory(raw_bytes, unit=MB, precision=0)
    bytes_per_token_str = fmt_int(bytes_per_token.to(byte / token).magnitude)
    window_tokens_str = fmt_int(window_tokens.to(token).magnitude)
    shaped_tokens_str = fmt_int(shaped_tokens.to(token).magnitude)
    remaining_turns_str = fmt_int(remaining_turns)
    input_price_str = fmt_usd((input_price * Mtoken).to(USD))
    cached_fraction_str = fmt_percent(cached_fraction_price, style="prose")
    raw_windows_mult_str = fmt_multiple(raw_windows, precision=1)
    shaped_share_str = fmt_percent(shaped_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    carried_cost_uncached_str = fmt_usd(carried_cost_uncached, precision=2)
    carried_cost_cached_str = fmt_usd(carried_cost_cached, precision=3)
    cached_discount_str = fmt_int(round(1 / cached_fraction_price))
    _mb = fmt(raw_bytes.to(MB).magnitude, precision=0, commas=False)
    _bpt = fmt_int(bytes_per_token.to(byte / token).magnitude)
    _tok = fmt_int(raw_tokens.to(token).magnitude).replace(",", "{,}")
    raw_tokens_math = fmt_math(rf"{_mb} \times 10^{{6}} / {_bpt} = {_tok}")
    _shaped = fmt_int(shaped_tokens.to(token).magnitude).replace(",", "{,}")
    _carried = fmt_int(carried_tokens.to(token).magnitude).replace(",", "{,}")
    carried_math = fmt_math(rf"{_shaped} \times {remaining_turns} = {_carried}")
```

::: {#nbk-07-observation-budget .callout-notebook title="The cost of carrying one observation through a trajectory"}
**Problem**: A hypothetical test log contains `{python} ObservationBudget.raw_size_str` of text. Assume, only for this estimate, `{python} ObservationBudget.bytes_per_token_str` bytes per token. The model's context window is `{python} ObservationBudget.window_tokens_str` tokens. The adapter instead produces a `{python} ObservationBudget.shaped_tokens_str`-token serialized observation, including its metadata, and the context policy selects that same payload for `{python} ObservationBudget.remaining_turns_str` later model calls. Assume input costs `{python} ObservationBudget.input_price_str` per million uncached tokens and cached input costs `{python} ObservationBudget.cached_fraction_str` of that price. What are the size and later input-cost consequences?

**Math**: Dividing the raw bytes by the assumed bytes per token gives `{python} ObservationBudget.raw_tokens_math` tokens, or `{python} ObservationBudget.raw_windows_mult_str` the entire window. The raw log cannot be admitted to this request. Actual tokenization depends on the specific vocabulary and input encoding; a coarse byte ratio serves for capacity planning rather than admission validation.

The shaped result occupies `{python} ObservationBudget.shaped_share_str` of the whole window, before accounting for other context and output reserve. Its later input contribution is `{python} ObservationBudget.carried_math` tokens. At the assumed prices, these later reads cost `{python} ObservationBudget.carried_cost_uncached_str` if all are uncached, or `{python} ObservationBudget.carried_cost_cached_str` if all qualify for cached-input billing. These figures exclude the initial inclusion, output generation, and all other request content.

**Systems insight**: Every staged observation incurs repeated token fees across subsequent turns that retain it in context. Its cumulative carried cost equals the serialized payload size multiplied by the remaining trajectory length. Systems engineers control both variables. Halving the staged payload or pruning the observation once the agent acts on its diagnostic cuts token expenditure proportionally, while prompt caching reduces costs by a factor of `{python} ObservationBudget.cached_discount_str` at current pricing tiers. Aggressive observation shaping directly lowers the amortized inference cost per accepted task, $C_{\text{eff}}$ (@sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic), provided the retained evidence remains sufficient for subsequent reasoning.
:::

### Truncation notices and inspection handles {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-truncation-notices}

When an observation is truncated, the metadata returned to the model must explicitly describe what was selected, what was omitted, and whether the missing data can still be retrieved. The runtime must distinguish between two fundamentally different operational states: a complete capture that was partially staged for prompt efficiency vs. an unrecoverable truncation where excess bytes were permanently dropped at the pipe boundary. Furthermore, omission metrics must reflect empirically measured quantities. If a stream dropped packets or terminated prematurely due to buffer overruns, the runtime should report that measurement uncertainty explicitly rather than fabricating an exact omitted byte count.

When storage policy permits retention, the runtime can spool the full raw output to an external artifact store and supply the model with an **inspection handle**\index{Inspection handle!definition}. Instead of re-executing an expensive build or test run to view omitted output, the agent can issue secondary queries such as `read_observation_slice(handle, offset_bytes, max_bytes)` to examine targeted slices. Alternatively, specialized tools can execute server-side regular expression searches over the retained log, returning only the lines surrounding a match alongside their exact byte offsets.

External artifact retention requires strict operational guardrails. Stored logs must be governed by explicit capacity quotas, eviction horizons, and clear error responses when a requested handle has expired or been evicted. Tool logs frequently contain sensitive data—such as environment variables, authorization tokens, or internal network paths—meaning artifact storage and secondary retrieval must enforce the same disclosure policies as primary tool execution. Cryptographic content hashes uniquely identify stored artifacts, but data integrity, read authorization, and storage durability remain distinct architectural responsibilities. When normalization transforms raw output (for example, stripping ANSI escape sequences or normalizing Unicode), the adapter must preserve byte-offset mappings so that subsequent range queries align correctly with the original text.

Structured tools can eliminate unmanageable payloads altogether by partitioning query results into discrete pages. A robust pagination interface enforces limits on both record count and serialized byte size, preventing single pathological records from overflowing the response. Each paginated response must communicate its boundary conditions: whether additional records remain, whether a backend execution deadline or scan limit truncated the search early, and what continuation token allows the client to resume. Pagination state is tracked through cursors. Because authorization and snapshot consistency operate independently, the API contract must clarify whether subsequent pages read from a frozen transaction snapshot or observe concurrent database modifications.

The placement of continuation state highlights a critical systems trade-off amplified by agentic workloads: stateful server-side cursors vs. stateless client tokens. A stateful cursor maintains an open database cursor, transaction snapshot, or cache entry on the server until the client finishes iterating. However, autonomous agents abandon search trajectories routinely; an informative diagnostic on the first page often redirects the agent's entire plan, causing abandoned server sessions to accumulate until garbage collection or time-to-live timeouts reclaim them. A **stateless cursor**\index{Stateless cursor!definition} avoids server-side state by encoding the continuation position directly within the token passed to the client. The backend serializes a query descriptor, the last evaluated sort key, and an issuance timestamp into a payload $d$, returning the authenticated token $d \parallel \text{MAC}_K(d)$ signed with a secret server key $K$. When the client returns the token, the backend verifies the message authentication code and expiration time, ensuring resistance against client-side tampering without consuming server memory. The trade-offs for stateless cursors are relaxed consistency and increased prompt overhead: resumption queries typically evaluate against live data rather than an isolated snapshot, and serialized cryptographic tokens consume valuable prompt tokens. Both approaches operationalize the retrieval-contract principles established in @sec-vol3-persistent-governance for agent tool execution.

Enforcing bounded capture and disciplined staging guarantees that tool output fits within allocated context budgets without exhausting host memory or deadlocking child processes. Securing that payload against semantic ambiguity and untrusted manipulation forms the subsequent layer of the tool execution runtime.

## Terminal Output Normalization {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-observation-parsing}

When a command-line tool executes interactively, it redraws progress indicators with carriage returns and styles diagnostics with terminal escape sequences. Captured directly at the byte level, standard output does not represent the clean visual layout a human engineer sees on a terminal screen. Wherever possible, tool adapters should invoke command-line utilities in noninteractive or batch modes (for example, `--batch` or `--no-color`), or ideally request structured machine-readable outputs such as JSON or JUnit XML. Structured reports provide discrete test identifiers, execution timings, and explicit assertions, eliminating the brittle heuristics required to parse colored progress logs. Even so, structured formatting is merely a transport convention; receiving a syntactically valid JSON payload does not guarantee that the tool performed all required checks or that its outputs can be trusted without schema validation and memory bounds.

When terminal output is unavoidable, the adapter must enforce a declared normalization policy backed by a stateful virtual terminal emulator or bounded screen buffer. Removing ANSI color sequences (`\x1b[31m`) is straightforward, but naively stripping control bytes like carriage returns (`\r`) or cursor positioning sequences silently corrupts output semantics.[^fn-terminal-control-functions] Because a carriage return moves the cursor to the beginning of the line without advancing to the next, a terminal progress indicator updates by repeatedly overwriting existing text. Stripping `\r` without simulating terminal geometry causes overwritten states to concatenate, turning `Running... \rFailed!` into `Running... Failed!` or accumulating megabytes of repeated progress fragments. The adapter's parser must therefore maintain cursor coordinates across chunked streaming reads while bounding its internal buffer allocations. When an adapter supports only a subset of control sequences, it must explicitly mark unsupported or incomplete escape sequences rather than discarding them silently. Because collapsing interactive updates into a final snapshot loses intermediate state transitions, the runtime should retain the raw byte stream in secondary storage as an authoritative audit log while delivering only the normalized, bounded representation to the model context.

[^fn-terminal-control-functions]: **Terminal Control Functions**: The escape sequences that color and reposition terminal text were standardized in ECMA-48, first published in 1976 and adopted internationally as ISO/IEC 6429 [@ecma1991control]. In that specification, carriage return moves the active position to the initial position of the line, allowing a terminal progress bar to overwrite the same line hundreds of times. A byte-level capture preserves every intermediate redraw; consequently, an interactive run that appears as a single line on screen can consume an agent's entire observation token budget unless the adapter interprets or collapses these control sequences. \index{ECMA-48!terminal normalization}

Tool adapters must preserve the provenance of standard output (`stdout`) and standard error (`stderr`) while treating stream assignments as advisory conventions. In Unix environments, programs frequently emit progress updates, debugging traces, or configuration warnings across either descriptor, and capturing the two streams through separate pipes forfeits their relative temporal interleaving. When chronological event ordering is essential for root-cause diagnosis, adapters should multiplex streams using pseudo-terminal (pty) pairs or timestamped chunk logging. In extracting diagnostics, the adapter should rely on known tool schemas—such as compiler error formats or language tracebacks—retaining source file paths and line offsets, while reporting parsing failures explicitly rather than guessing a root cause from an incomplete fragment. Normalizing terminal output cleans up presentation, but the resulting text carries no intrinsic authority. Safe serialization practices, including escaping control characters and enforcing UTF-8 boundaries, protect the agent's structural messaging format from delimiter injection, while the evidence-scope rule continues to dictate what the text actually proves.

### Process status and evidential scope {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-process-status}

The adapter must determine process disposition directly from operating system primitives—such as `waitpid` status macros or container runtime lifecycle events—rather than parsing success messages from output logs. Querying the process supervisor allows the adapter to report an unambiguous exit code,[^fn-exit-status-bits] an unhandled terminating signal, or a timeout without textual speculation. Observing an end-of-file condition on standard streams does not prove that a process has completed its work: a daemon or worker process can close its inherited descriptors while continuing to execute asynchronously in the background. Conversely, a broken communication socket or interrupted execution channel leaves the state of any requested side effects uncertain.

[^fn-exit-status-bits]: **Eight-Bit Exit Status**: Under POSIX semantics, a parent process inspects child termination through status macros like `WIFEXITED` and `WEXITSTATUS`, which yield only the low-order eight bits (values 0–255) of the argument passed to `exit`. A program that terminates with exit code 256 wraps modulo 256 and appears to the parent as exit status 0. Furthermore, standard shells synthesize synthetic return codes above 128 when a process is killed by a signal (for example, 137 for `SIGKILL` 9 or 139 for `SIGSEGV` 11), collapsing fatal OS signals into ambiguous numerical exit statuses. An adapter that records explicit disposition variants—such as `exited(code)` vs. `signaled(sig)`—avoids truncating or conflating these conditions. \index{Exit status!POSIX}

An exit status of zero is an application convention rather than definitive proof that every required validation ran to completion. Three recurring systems failures illustrate this divergence. First, a test runner pointed at an incorrect directory path or unmatched pattern filter may discover zero tests and exit cleanly with status 0. Second, a shell script executed without `set -e` and `set -o pipefail` can suffer a fatal failure in an early command yet still return status 0 because the final pipeline stage succeeds. Third, an API client can catch an internal runtime exception, print the error payload to standard output, and terminate with code 0 because the transport exchange itself finished without an unhandled crash. Under the evidence-scope rule, the adapter treats the operating system process status as a single evidentiary signal. It correlates this status with structured output payloads and the specific acceptance criteria defined by the task. In a connection-pool repair, for instance, confirming that a targeted reproduction test passes on workspace revision `r18` proves only that the reproducer succeeded; it does not substantiate broader system stability or justify full patch acceptance.

@Lst-vol3-observation-sanitization illustrates this distinction. In this scenario, the adapter executed a targeted test against an explicit workspace snapshot (`r18`), parsed its structured assertions, and captured the full output stream within its retention budget. Only a bounded summary is staged into the prompt context. These fields represent an illustrative adapter contract rather than an immutable tool schema.

::: {#lst-vol3-observation-sanitization lst-cap="**A bounded result with scoped evidence**: Process disposition, tested source, check outcome, and observation completeness answer different questions."}
```json
{
  "call_id": "call_test_42",
  "scope": {"repository": "repair-workspace", "revision": "r18"},
  "process": {"state": "exited", "exit_code": 0},
  "check": {
    "target": "tests/test_pool.py::test_waiter_notified_on_return",
    "outcome": "passed",
    "broader_regression_checks": "not_run"
  },
  "observation": {
    "capture": "complete",
    "staged_view": "excerpt",
    "selection": "invocation header and final test summary",
    "text": "Target: tests/test_pool.py::test_waiter_notified_on_return\n[intermediate output omitted]\nResult: passed",
    "omission_notice": "Intermediate output omitted from this view.",
    "inspection_handle": "obs_42",
    "retention": "until this task ends"
  }
}
```
:::

The fields in @lst-vol3-observation-sanitization separate process status from evidentiary scope. The `call_id` correlates this result with a specific interaction turn. The `scope` block pins the result to workspace revision `r18`, preventing execution evidence from floating across different repository commits. Under `check`, the adapter confirms that the single reproducer succeeded while explicitly recording that broader regression suites remain unexecuted. In parallel, the `observation` block reports capture completeness: while the full execution log was preserved, the prompt context receives only an excerpt containing the header and summary verdict. The runtime exposes `obs_42` as an inspection handle so the model can request paginated log windows if deeper analysis is needed. The runtime mediates all operations on `obs_42`, ensuring that knowing the handle's string grants no ambient authority across session boundaries.[^fn-handle-capability-tools] If resource limits had forced the adapter to truncate collection early, the payload would mark `capture` as incomplete and indicate which byte ranges remain available for inspection.

[^fn-handle-capability-tools]: **Names vs. Capabilities**: Dennis and Van Horn's foundational capability model granted authority through possession of an unforgeable ticket or reference [@dennis1966]. Agent runtime architectures intentionally stop short of treating context-visible observation handles as capabilities. Because text in a model's context window can be logged, leaked, copied by prompt injections, or replayed across user boundaries, the runtime treats an inspection handle merely as an identifier (a name). The runtime verifies caller authorization and execution scope on each access, ensuring that possessing a handle string grants no ambient authority. \index{Capability!handles versus names}

::: {#chk-07-idempotency-recovery .callout-checkpoint title="Interpreting uncertain effects and bounded observations"}

- [ ] **Delayed attempt**: A restart times out, and a later probe sees the old state. The first attempt may still commit. What additional guarantee or evidence is needed before repeating the restart?
- [ ] **Duplicate rate**: In notebook \ref{nbk-07-settlement-budget}, reply loss doubles while request loss stays fixed. Roughly how does the daily duplicate count change, and which single change removes that path instead of shrinking it?
- [ ] **Omitted evidence**: A known failed test run has a complete retained log but only a head-and-tail excerpt in context. What can the agent infer from the absent stack trace, and what bounded inspection should it request?
- [ ] **Scoped status**: The result above reports exit code zero and one targeted pass on `r18`. Which claims does that support, and which acceptance questions remain open?
- [ ] **Instruction-like output**: A normalized log contains an instruction to upload the repository elsewhere. Which presentation checks have occurred, and why do they grant no authority for that proposed upload?

:::

Synchronous tool execution assumes the adapter can resolve process status, normalize terminal streams, and package evidence within the span of a single model turn. When operations run longer than conversational deadlines allow, asynchronous dispatch extends this same return-path contract to running jobs—tracking process lifecycles and staging bounded observations without mistaking initial dispatch for completion.

## Asynchronous Tool Dispatch {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-async}

When an automated repair agent launches an extensive regression test suite, it rarely has any useful decision to make until the results arrive. A prompt return from that tool invocation functions merely as an acknowledgment of receipt; the actual computation has only just begun. During the intervening minutes or hours, the agent runtime must supervise background execution, enforce resource budgets, and maintain system safety without freezing its control plane or burning inference tokens on idle waiting.

### Synchronous and asynchronous interfaces {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-mismatch}

A synchronous tool interface blocks until execution finishes and returns its final result directly to the caller. This approach works well for sub-second database lookups, local arithmetic, or deterministic queries where the agent cannot proceed without the answer. Even during a synchronous wait, a well-structured runtime does not freeze its control plane; background worker threads can still monitor process heartbeats, stream partial standard output, and enforce timeouts. System fragility emerges when synchronous waiting binds the supervisor thread directly to child process completion, leaving the host unable to respond to cancellation signals or reclaim runaway resources.

An asynchronous interface decouples job submission from job completion. Rather than waiting for the underlying process to exit, the dispatch call immediately returns a handle representing the pending task, alongside methods to inspect its status, stream intermediate observations, or await termination. This separation allows the agent trajectory to suspend cleanly without burning model inference cycles, or to continue executing independent tasks concurrently. However, concurrent execution introduces data consistency hazards. If an agent modifies `src/pool.py` while a background test suite reads from the working tree, the resulting test outcome reflects an ambiguous mix of revisions unless the runtime isolates the background job within a fixed snapshot or a copy-on-write workspace. Asynchronous execution increases concurrency, but it demands strict workspace isolation to prevent silent data corruption.

Decoupling task execution from model inference also clarifies how the runtime manages inference serving state. While a background job runs, the model requires no token generation. The inference serving engine can retain, offload, or evict compatible KV cache state under its own paging policies, completely independent of the tool's lifecycle. When the background job completes and the agent trajectory resumes, the runtime constructs the subsequent prompt context. Keeping an open HTTP connection or hanging synchronous socket throughout a long build provides no caching guarantees and merely holds host network resources hostage. Attention state can either be recomputed over the prompt prefix or restored from a prefix cache according to the serving engine's eviction state.

### Job handles {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-escrow}

The runtime admits a proposed asynchronous call using the same validation, authorization, and resource checks required for synchronous invocation. If the executor accepts the work, the runtime records the job's identity, owner, requested operation, applicable source revision, execution limits, and observation location. A model-visible **job handle**\index{Job handle!definition} identifies that record without exposing the executor's internal process-management interface. Under the principle of least privilege, status reads, output inspection, interactive input, and cancellation each require their own explicit authorization checks.

A provider-neutral acknowledgment might be:

```json
{
  "call_id": "call_tests_1",
  "status": "accepted_pending",
  "job_id": "job_tests_18",
  "source_revision": "r18",
  "result_available": false
}
```

Here `call_id` correlates the dispatch exchange, while `job_id` identifies the accepted work for later interactions. If a mutating operation also requires a logical operation ID for retry handling, that identity retains the idempotency semantics established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency; a job ID alone supplies no deduplication guarantee. Dropping the dispatch reply across an unreliable network leaves the runtime uncertain whether the executor accepted the task, mirroring the ambiguity of a timeout during a synchronous call.

This initial acknowledgment confirms only that the executor accepted the request into its work queue; it makes no claims about whether the process has started running or whether tests have passed. Subsequent status queries can report active execution, an explicit request for user input, completion with a structured result, or failure with diagnostic details. If network partitions or host restarts make the executor temporarily unreachable, returning “last observed running” alongside “current status unavailable” preserves critical operational context. Reporting an unconfirmed status as an outright failure causes agents to trigger mistaken rollbacks, because a timeout while polling status does not mean the background process stopped executing.

When the result becomes available, the runtime delivers the bounded observation contract, specifying the tested revision, the checks actually executed, the process exit disposition, and any output truncation. For example, a completed test job at revision `r18` can report that `test_waiter_notified_on_return` passed. Furthermore, because a child process can exit cleanly while an output buffer truncates under heavy logging, process termination and output completeness remain distinct fields in the observation contract.

### Resumption mechanisms {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-resumption}

Systems track asynchronous job state through several mechanisms, distinguished primarily by whether state detection requires model inference. @Tbl-vol3-resumption-mechanisms compares the three primary patterns.

| Mechanism                           | Who checks or reports status?                         | When model inference is useful                                      |
|:------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Model-directed inspection           | The model proposes a bounded status or output request | A new observation may change the diagnosis or next action           |
| Runtime polling                     | The runtime checks on a bounded schedule              | A reported change requires a decision or the final result is ready  |
| Completion or progress notification | The executor signals a relevant event to the runtime  | The runtime has obtained evidence sufficient to resume deliberation |

: **Resumption choices**: Waiting and status detection can occur outside model inference; deliberate inspection remains useful when it informs a decision. {#tbl-vol3-resumption-mechanisms}

Repeated model-directed polling imposes severe financial and computational penalties when successive checks return identical "still running" responses. By delegating health checks to the runtime, systems avoid redundant inference calls while retaining simple polling semantics. Event-driven notifications (such as webhooks or message queues) further eliminate polling traffic between the runtime and the executor, though they introduce operational complexity: the runtime must authenticate callbacks, correlate incoming events with job identifiers, and handle dropped, delayed, or duplicated deliveries. In practice, receiving a completion notification often acts as a trigger for the runtime to execute a validated status read, rather than treating the notification payload itself as authoritative proof of completion. Both polling and notification architectures require dedicated supervisory resources; preserving pending jobs across runtime host failures is developed in @sec-vol3-durable-execution.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-tool-calling-polling
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EXTRA MODEL CALLS WHILE A JOB IS PENDING
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-07-token-cost-and-inference-overhead.
# │ Goal: Isolate model-driven status overhead under equal useful work.
# │ Show: Pending call count, input/output tokens, and incremental token cost.
# │ How: Count scheduled checks strictly before completion; apply hypothetical
# │      cached/uncached input and output prices. Exclude common useful calls.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *

class PollingBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario assumptions) ──────────────────────────────────
    job_duration = Q_(300, "second")  # hypothetical fixed completion time
    poll_interval = Q_(5, "second")  # checks start one interval after dispatch
    context_tokens = 32_768  # selected input per status call, including prior status
    output_tokens_per_call = 40  # complete generated status request; no extra acknowledgment
    cache_fraction = 0.95  # hypothetical aggregate input fraction billed as cached
    input_price_per_mtok = 3.00  # hypothetical dollars per million uncached input tokens
    cached_price_per_mtok = 0.30  # hypothetical dollars per million cached input tokens
    output_price_per_mtok = 15.00  # hypothetical dollars per million generated tokens

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    pending_calls = math.ceil((job_duration / poll_interval).to("").magnitude) - 1
    total_input_tokens = pending_calls * context_tokens
    total_output_tokens = pending_calls * output_tokens_per_call
    blended_input_price = (1 - cache_fraction) * input_price_per_mtok + cache_fraction * cached_price_per_mtok
    input_cost = total_input_tokens / 1e6 * blended_input_price
    output_cost = total_output_tokens / 1e6 * output_price_per_mtok
    extra_cost = input_cost + output_cost

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Prose claims) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pending_calls == 59, "Only scheduled checks strictly before completion count")
    check(total_input_tokens == 1_933_312, "Input includes exactly the pending calls")
    check(total_output_tokens == 2_360, "No separate generated acknowledgment is charged")
    check(abs(extra_cost - 0.87639072) < 1e-8, "Incremental token cost under stated prices")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    job_s_str = fmt_time(job_duration, unit="second", precision=0)
    interval_s_str = fmt_time(poll_interval, unit="second", precision=0)
    context_tokens_str = fmt_tokens(context_tokens)
    output_tokens_per_call_str = fmt_tokens(output_tokens_per_call)
    cache_pct_str = fmt_percent(cache_fraction, style="prose")
    input_price_str = fmt_usd(input_price_per_mtok, precision=0)
    cached_price_str = fmt_usd(cached_price_per_mtok, precision=2)
    output_price_str = fmt_usd(output_price_per_mtok, precision=0)
    pending_calls_str = fmt_count(pending_calls)
    total_input_tokens_str = fmt_tokens(total_input_tokens)
    total_output_tokens_str = fmt_tokens(total_output_tokens)
    input_cost_str = fmt_usd(input_cost, precision=4)
    output_cost_str = fmt_usd(output_cost, precision=4)
    extra_cost_str = fmt_usd(extra_cost, precision=4)
```

::: {#nbk-07-token-cost-and-inference-overhead .callout-notebook title="The extra cost of asking whether a job finished"}

**Problem**: A background test job completes in `{python} PollingBudget.job_s_str`. Under a model-directed polling strategy, the agent queries status every `{python} PollingBudget.interval_s_str`, starting one interval after dispatch and ending strictly before completion. Assume each status check finishes before the next scheduled query and does not alter overall execution time. Each model invocation consumes a `{python} PollingBudget.context_tokens_str`-token prompt (including preceding status history) and generates a `{python} PollingBudget.output_tokens_per_call_str`-token query, with no additional model acknowledgment required. What incremental inference overhead does this polling loop impose compared to event-driven runtime detection?

**Math**: Because both architectures execute the initial dispatch and the final completion invocation, we exclude those shared calls. The polling schedule produces `{python} PollingBudget.pending_calls_str` intermediate model invocations, consuming `{python} PollingBudget.total_input_tokens_str` input tokens and `{python} PollingBudget.total_output_tokens_str` generated tokens. The selected context length remains fixed across queries rather than accumulating unbounded history.

Assume `{python} PollingBudget.cache_pct_str` of input tokens qualify for prompt caching discounts, priced at `{python} PollingBudget.cached_price_str` per million tokens vs. `{python} PollingBudget.input_price_str` per million uncached tokens, with generation billed at `{python} PollingBudget.output_price_str` per million tokens. Multiplying token counts by their respective rates yields `{python} PollingBudget.input_cost_str` in input charges and `{python} PollingBudget.output_cost_str` in output charges, producing `{python} PollingBudget.extra_cost_str` of direct inference overhead per background job.

**Systems insight**: The monetary overhead of model-driven polling scales linearly with job duration and inversely with polling interval: $(\text{duration} / \text{interval}) \times \text{tokens} \times \text{price}$. Halving the poll interval doubles the expenditure. Adding `{python} PollingBudget.extra_cost_str` to every pending task directly inflates the attempt cost in the numerator of effective cost $C_{\text{eff}}$, paying for status information that the host runtime can monitor at near-zero cost. Systems should delegate routine state tracking to the runtime harness, waking the model only when incoming observations require fresh architectural deliberation.

:::

### Job supervision and cancellation {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-governance}

Background execution retains a defined owner and security boundary. While the model trajectory pauses, the runtime continues enforcing the job's execution deadline, resource ceilings, output budgets, and permissible external side effects. Bounded inspection requests return the latest status alongside a selected slice of output annotated with capture timestamps and truncation metadata. When a job's log output goes silent, the runtime cannot immediately assume deadlock; an explicit status signal or targeted diagnostic probe is necessary to distinguish between slow computation, blocked I/O waiting for user input, or an abandoned worker process.

Some tools require interactive input during execution. Wherever possible, runtimes should configure tools in non-interactive modes with complete parameters passed at invocation. When interaction is unavoidable, an explicit adapter event or structured protocol message must declare what input the job expects. Operating-system process sleep states provide no semantic insight into what prompt or data the child process awaits. Before forwarding input from an agent, the runtime must validate current job state, confirm input semantics, and re-check permission grants. For instance, answering "yes" to a database migration prompt can trigger destructive schema mutations that exceed an agent's original read-only inspection grant.

Cancellation is an asynchronous control action with distinct intermediate states rather than an instantaneous rollback. When requested, the runtime acknowledges receipt of the cancellation signal and subsequently records the outcome reported by the executor. The job may stop cleanly, complete before the signal arrives, reject the cancellation request, or become unreachable with termination unconfirmed. An expiring timeout deadline triggers an identical supervisory intervention and audit trail. The runtime remains responsible for tracking and reclaiming every supervised descendant process and remote resource within its containment boundary.

On a POSIX host, that boundary for a local command is typically a **process group**\index{POSIX process group!definition}, which establishes the set of processes reached by a single signal. A tool that executes `bash -c "make && pytest"` spawns a shell, which in turn spawns `make`, compiler subprocesses, the test runner, and multiple worker threads or forks. Signaling only the top-level shell process terminates the shell, but leaves orphaned descendants reparented to the system init process (`PID 1`). These orphaned processes continue consuming CPU cycles, holding file system locks, and keeping socket descriptors open. To prevent orphan leaks, the execution adapter configures each job as the leader of its own process group at spawn time—calling `setpgid(0, 0)` in the child before invoking `exec`—and directs all signals to the entire group. It sends `SIGTERM` first, granting processes a bounded grace period to flush buffers and release external resources, followed by an uncatchable `SIGKILL`. @Lst-vol3-process-group-teardown implements this escalation pattern and reports the verified outcome. If an untrusted process deliberately creates a new session or process group to escape group signaling, the runtime must rely on the kernel-level isolation boundaries discussed in @sec-vol3-sandboxes.

::: {#lst-vol3-process-group-teardown lst-cap="**Process-group teardown with escalation**: The job leads its own group, so one signal reaches every descendant still in it. Liveness is probed with signal 0 after reaping exited children, and a group that survives `SIGKILL` is reported as unconfirmed rather than assumed stopped."}
```python
import os, signal, subprocess, time

def spawn_job(argv):
    proc = subprocess.Popen(argv, process_group=0)  # setpgid(0, 0)
    return proc.pid                  # the leader's PID is the group ID

def group_alive(pgid):
    try:                             # reap exited children of ours,
        while os.waitpid(-pgid, os.WNOHANG)[0] > 0:  # or zombies
            pass                                     # still count
    except ChildProcessError:        # no children of ours remain
        pass
    try:
        os.killpg(pgid, 0)           # signal 0 probes, delivers nothing
        return True
    except ProcessLookupError:
        return False

def terminate_group(pgid, grace_s=3.0):
    for sig, wait_s in ((signal.SIGTERM, grace_s), (signal.SIGKILL, 1.0)):
        try:
            os.killpg(pgid, sig)
        except ProcessLookupError:   # group already gone
            return "exited" if sig == signal.SIGTERM else "terminated"
        deadline = time.monotonic() + wait_s
        while time.monotonic() < deadline:
            if not group_alive(pgid):
                return "terminated" if sig == signal.SIGTERM else "killed"
            time.sleep(0.05)
    return "unconfirmed"             # report it; do not claim a stop
```
:::

Two subtle POSIX semantics govern the correctness of this routine. First, when invoking non-blocking `os.waitpid(-pgid, os.WNOHANG)`, a return value of zero indicates that child processes still exist in the group and none has changed state yet; it does not indicate that the process group has cleared. The runtime continues reaping until no direct child processes remain, at which point the system call raises `ChildProcessError`. Second, sending signal 0 via `os.killpg(pgid, 0)` delivers no actual signal to the target group; the kernel simply performs error checking, confirming whether any process matching that group ID still exists and is accessible. Probing with signal 0 directly determines whether any group member remains alive after signal delivery.

Even when process termination is confirmed, stopping an execution does not roll back side effects that occurred before the signal arrived. A canceled deployment script may already have mutated external cloud resources, and a canceled test run may leave temporary database tables behind. The final observation emitted by the runtime must record all known side effects, pending cleanup obligations, and ambiguous states. In the system's execution ledger, a status of "canceled" confirms that execution halted; it does not signify that the system returned to its original state. How execution boundaries constrain damage is developed in @sec-vol3-sandboxes, while handling interrupted workflows and partial mutations is analyzed in @sec-vol3-failure-recovery.

An asynchronous tool interface thus preserves the invariant guarantees of tool execution across extended time horizons: it acknowledges queued work without stalling the client, enforces strict resource boundaries, emits bounded observations, and distinguishes requested operations from confirmed system states. Managing complex toolkits over time ultimately requires structuring tool sets so that long-running operations and their corresponding inspection handles form a coherent, self-consistent operational surface.

## Designing the Active Toolkit {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-toolkit-design}

An agent diagnosing and repairing an exhausted database connection pool requires concrete operations: inspecting source files, applying candidate patches, executing test suites, and analyzing run-time diagnostics. Toolkit design governs how an agent runtime exposes these capabilities to the foundation model. If an interface exposes too little functionality per invocation, the model must coordinate low-level state across dozens of turns; if it exposes an unconstrained catalog, the context window fills with irrelevant tool schemas that bloat prefill latency and degrade decision quality. The goal of toolkit design is to expose operations so that the model can choose an appropriate next step without carrying unnecessary definitions or managing avoidable intermediate state.

Two design dimensions govern this trade-off. Granularity determines how much work an individual tool performs, while catalog selection determines which subset of tool definitions the model sees on any given turn, known as the **active toolkit**\index{Active toolkit!definition}. A small catalog can contain either narrowly bounded primitives or a broadly expressive command runner, whereas an enterprise environment registering hundreds of specialized tools must stage them selectively rather than presenting the entire catalog on every turn.

### Static and on-demand staging {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-tool-staging}

In **static staging**\index{Tool staging!static}, the runtime serializes a fixed set of tool descriptors into every request. This keeps available interfaces predictable and eliminates separate discovery steps when a task requires a specific tool. The operational cost is wasted input capacity: every descriptor consumes context tokens on every turn, regardless of whether that capability is relevant to the immediate decision. In contrast, **on-demand staging**\index{Tool staging!on-demand} dynamically selects descriptors as the trajectory unfolds. This reduces the prompt footprint and prefill latency, but it introduces the operational risk that a critical tool is omitted or discovered late, forcing the agent to expend extra turns locating it.

Selection mechanisms vary widely in implementation complexity. A runtime can employ deterministic task-to-tool mappings, hierarchical namespace menus, keyword matching, dense vector retrieval, or a combination of these approaches. Dense retrieval represents one possible search technique rather than a universal requirement for large catalogs. As with the retrieval methods in @sec-vol3-long-term-memory, any match returned by a retriever is merely a candidate descriptor. A robust systems design provides a bounded fallback path—such as a dedicated tool-search operation or an explicit discovery failure signal—so that an omitted descriptor does not cause the model to conclude erroneously that the operation cannot be performed.

Staging a descriptor makes its syntactic and semantic contract visible to the model; under the grant rule, staging confers no execution privileges. The runtime must still resolve and authenticate every proposed invocation against registered tool identities and permissions before execution. If a dynamic discovery step returns a modified or re-versioned descriptor, the runtime must reconcile that version before executing it, preventing the model from dispatching against an interface different from the one it was provided.

Tool definitions consume prompt capacity alongside system instructions, source excerpts, previous observations, and generation headroom. Systems engineers must measure the final serialized request, including formatting delimiters, wrapper schemas, and selection metadata, rather than tallying independently tokenized description fragments under the false assumption that token boundaries are free. The following ledger isolates catalog-related input for an individual model request.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/tool_calling_margin_catalog_budget.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars drawn to scale. The full-catalog bar is solid. The selected bar is a short descriptor segment plus a thin selection-overhead segment, with the remaining length outlined and labeled released."}

*Selection frees most of the catalog's input, on every call.*
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: calc-vol3-toolkit-catalog-budget
# What: Compare catalog-related input in one hypothetical model request.
# How: Charge full descriptors in both layouts and explicit additional
#      selection/framing tokens in the selected layout. No hardware estimate.
from mlsysim import *

class ToolkitCatalogBudget:
    # 1. LOAD — stipulated counts in final serialization, not tokenizer laws.
    registered_tools = 50
    selected_tools = 6
    tokens_per_descriptor = 300 * count
    selection_overhead = 400 * count

    # 2. EXECUTE — other request content is held fixed and excluded here.
    static_tokens = registered_tools * tokens_per_descriptor
    selected_descriptors = selected_tools * tokens_per_descriptor
    selected_total = selected_descriptors + selection_overhead
    released_capacity = static_tokens - selected_total
    unused_descriptors = (registered_tools - selected_tools) * tokens_per_descriptor
    breakeven_unused = (selection_overhead / tokens_per_descriptor).to("").magnitude

    # 3. GUARD — compare the same descriptors and include added overhead.
    check(0 < selected_tools < registered_tools, "Selected tools form a proper subset")
    check(static_tokens == 15_000 * count, "Full catalog count must balance")
    check(selected_total == 2_200 * count, "Selected count includes selection overhead")
    check(selected_total + released_capacity == static_tokens, "Capacity ledger must balance")
    check(unused_descriptors == 13_200 * count, "Unused descriptors removed by selection")
    check(1 < breakeven_unused < 2, "Selection pays once two unused descriptors are removed")

    # 4. OUTPUT — typed counts and token formatters for every visible input/result.
    registered_tools_str = fmt_count(registered_tools * count)
    selected_tools_str = fmt_count(selected_tools * count)
    tokens_per_descriptor_str = fmt_tokens(tokens_per_descriptor)
    selection_overhead_str = fmt_tokens(selection_overhead)
    static_tokens_str = fmt_tokens(static_tokens)
    selected_total_str = fmt_tokens(selected_total)
    unused_descriptors_str = fmt_tokens(unused_descriptors)
    breakeven_unused_str = fmt(breakeven_unused, precision=1)
    _n = lambda q: fmt_int(q.to(count).magnitude).replace(",", "{,}")
    static_math = fmt_math(rf"{registered_tools} \times {_n(tokens_per_descriptor)} = {_n(static_tokens)}")
    selected_math = fmt_math(rf"{selected_tools} \times {_n(tokens_per_descriptor)} + {_n(selection_overhead)} = {_n(selected_total)}")
    released_math = fmt_math(rf"{_n(static_tokens)} - {_n(selected_total)} = {_n(released_capacity)}")
```

::: {#nbk-07-memory-footprint-and-prefill-latency .callout-notebook title="The input budget of an active catalog"}

**Problem**: How much next-call input capacity does a selected catalog release after counting its additional framing and selection information?

**Variables**: Suppose a registered catalog has `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.registered_tools_str` tools. Each complete descriptor contributes `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.tokens_per_descriptor_str` tokens, including its share of catalog framing. The alternative stages `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.selected_tools_str` of the same descriptors plus `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.selection_overhead_str` additional tokens for the selection interface and metadata. These are stipulated contributions within the final serialization, with other request content unchanged. In this scenario the runtime selects the subset without another model call.

**Math**: Full staging uses `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.static_math` tokens. The selected descriptors plus selection overhead use `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.selected_math` tokens. The released capacity is therefore `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.released_math` tokens.

**Systems insight**: Selection pays whenever its overhead is smaller than the unused descriptors it removes, here `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.selection_overhead_str` against `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.unused_descriptors_str` tokens; break-even sits at about `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.breakeven_unused_str` unused descriptors, so the saving grows linearly with catalog size. The released capacity recurs on every call that would have carried the full catalog, so over a trajectory it multiplies by the number of turns, like the carried observation in notebook \ref{nbk-07-observation-budget}. The comparison flips when selection needs its own model call or a missed tool forces rediscovery; those calls belong in the same ledger.

:::

Static and selected catalogs also interact differently with prefix caching in serving runtimes. When an inference engine leverages radix-tree or hash-based KV cache reuse, maintaining an identical serialized prefix across turns allows the engine to bypass prefill computation for earlier prompt segments. Static staging preserves a stable prompt prefix across calls, maximizing cache reuse as long as earlier conversation state remains intact. Conversely, modifying descriptors or reordering them across turns moves the point of prompt divergence earlier, invalidating downstream cached KV blocks and forcing redundant prefill computation (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging and @sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree). A hybrid strategy places an immutable core of common descriptors early in the prompt and appends task-specific additions later. Even so, systems designers must not retain obsolete or revoked definitions merely to retain a cache hit, as doing so exposes outdated interfaces to the model. Furthermore, removing an earlier temporary tool definition alters the prompt prefix for subsequent turns, invalidating the cached state of the assistant responses and observations that followed it.

### Tool granularity {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-granularity}

Tool granularity governs how much operational work is encapsulated within a single tool call vs. how much intermediate coordination is offloaded to the model across multiple turns. Classic systems modularity principles apply directly here. Parnas established that effective module boundaries hide design decisions that are subject to change [@parnas1972criteria], and Ousterhout formalized this criterion through deep vs. shallow interfaces, measuring how much implementation complexity an abstraction hides relative to the surface area it exposes [@ousterhout2018philosophy]. Empirical studies confirm these principles in agent systems: designing tool interfaces tailored to an agent's editing, navigation, and testing patterns significantly improves task success rates on software engineering benchmarks [@yang2024sweagent]. A **deep interface**\index{Deep interface!definition} encapsulates substantial functionality behind a concise contract, whereas a shallow interface exposes almost as much complexity as it implements. For example, a file-editing interface built from discrete `open_file`, `seek_cursor`, `write_bytes`, and `close_file` operations forces the model to manage low-level file descriptors, cursor offsets, and resource cleanup across the trajectory. Such fine-grained decomposition is warranted only when intermediate inspection is an explicit requirement; when the agent merely intends to apply a bounded patch, this overhead invites state corruption and premature failure.

A task-level patch operation moves mechanical file manipulation behind the tool implementation, returning a unified diff, a resulting version hash, or an explicit conflict. The conditional-edit contract in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-schemas illustrates this boundary. However, interface naming alone does not guarantee transactional safety: if an operation advertises all-or-nothing execution, the underlying implementation must enforce that atomicity across its mutation scope and failure modes. When operations span multiple files or distributed endpoints, partial side effects become inevitable, and the runtime must report those partial outcomes explicitly in the tool observation. Bundling multi-step work into a single tool call reallocates responsibility from model planning to runtime execution, but the underlying systems obligations remain intact. @Fig-vol3-deep-vs-shallow-interface contrasts these two interface granularities for the same file modification: low-level primitive tools (panel a) require four sequential model turns (open, seek, write, close) that inflate token overhead and invite race conditions, whereas a high-level atomic edit tool (panel b) executes targeted find-and-replace within the sandbox in a single turn.

::: {#fig-vol3-deep-vs-shallow-interface fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Shallow and deep interfaces for one edit**: The low-level composition (a) spends four model calls and places a handle, a cursor, and cleanup in the trajectory between them. The task-level operation (b) spends one call and moves the version check and the change behind the interface, returning either a diff with its new version or a version conflict. The deeper interface is all-or-nothing only if its implementation provides that property; either way, the obligations move rather than disappear." fig-alt="Two side-by-side panels. Panel a, low-level composition, shows four rows, each with a model call, a tool call, and a result in context: open_file returns a handle, seek_cursor returns a cursor position, write_bytes returns bytes written, and close_file returns closed. Below, the model selects each operation and carries handles and cleanup, while the implementation validates each operation. Panel b, task-level operation, shows one model call to apply_patch with path, expected version, and patch, an implementation box that checks the version then applies the change, noted as all-or-nothing only if the implementation provides it, and two possible results: diff and new version, or version conflict. Below, the model states one bounded intent and the implementation enforces the precondition and mutation boundary."}
![](images/svg/deep_vs_shallow_tool_interface.svg)
:::

Careful toolkit design does not require eliminating all overlapping capabilities. A system can effectively combine a structured search tool that returns AST matches with an authorized shell runner that supports complex log analysis beyond the search tool's schema. To prevent model confusion, their descriptors must articulate clear functional boundaries, target inputs, and operational limits. Providing duplicate tools with near-identical names and indistinguishable schemas adds selection noise without expanding capability; in contrast, providing complementary interfaces with distinct observation formats, coverage scopes, or authorization grants offers substantial utility. @Tbl-vol3-toolkit-granularity summarizes how these interface styles partition responsibility between the model and runtime.

| Interface style                   | Work assigned to the model                                   | Work assigned to the implementation                                                           |
|:----------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Low-level composition             | Select intermediate operations and manage their dependencies | Validate each operation and expose handle, status, and cleanup semantics.                     |
| Task-level operation              | Specify a bounded intent, such as a patch or a test target   | Implement preconditions, mutation boundaries, and interpretable results for that task.        |
| General command or program runner | Construct a program that expresses the intended work         | Enforce execution grants and resource limits, supervise the job, and return bounded evidence. |

: **Toolkit granularity and responsibility**: Broader composition and task-specific interfaces place different obligations on the model and implementation; neither column substitutes for authorization or containment. {#tbl-vol3-toolkit-granularity tbl-colwidths="[24,33,43]"}

An argument schema constrains the syntactic format of a request, but it cannot constrain the underlying code execution. A specialized symbol-renaming tool may parse external ASTs, inspect secondary source trees, or execute defective third-party libraries. A narrow signature provides safety only when the implementation and its surrounding execution sandbox enforce that advertised boundary. Conversely, a shell runner's blast radius is defined by its working directory, operating-system privileges, credential access, and network egress rules. Because the side effects of an expressive shell command cannot be reliably determined by inspecting its arguments, the runtime must rely on containment to enforce isolation (@sec-vol3-sandboxes).

Tool implementations should also adopt defensive defaults grounded in physical systems behavior. When an agent provides an ambiguous file path or target identifier, rejecting the call with an informative diagnostic is far safer than guessing or silently appending data, as appending is a stateful mutation that can silently duplicate configuration entries. A dry-run mode allows the model to inspect a proposed diff against the current workspace state before committing changes; the runtime must still enforce approval gates and verify preconditions at execution time. These defensive defaults make operational failures interpretable, but engineers should remember that rollback capabilities and high-fidelity simulation are properties of the underlying tool implementation, not inherent guarantees of the interface.

### Catalog evaluation {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-catalog-evaluation}

Rigorous evaluation of toolkit designs requires isolating the effects of granularity and staging policy by holding all other experimental factors constant: the benchmark task distribution, initial workspace snapshots, model checkpoints, generation parameters, token budgets, and verification suites. In the connection-pool repair workload, test trials must exercise realistic failure modes: locating relevant source files across deep directory hierarchies, applying patches against concurrently modified buffers, interpreting noisy test failure logs, and recovering gracefully when a necessary tool descriptor is omitted from the initial active toolkit. These targeted trials disentangle catalog coverage limitations from model selection errors, and separate model selection accuracy from execution-time runtime failures.

Comprehensive evaluation logs must record selection errors, malformed arguments, rejected preconditions, unnecessary discovery calls, recovery turns, and uncontained side effects alongside binary task completion. Cost accounting should measure serialized descriptor tokens, retrieval and reranking latency, execution sandbox compute time, observation overhead, and cumulative tokens wasted on failed trajectories. A recovered tool selection error costs inference turns and latency, whereas an unrecovered error aborts the task; consequently, toolkits are ranked by total cost per accepted task rather than the simple probability of avoiding selection errors. Furthermore, when comparing designs that require fundamentally different security postures—such as an unconstrained command runner vs. a constrained AST manipulation tool—evaluations must report those privilege differences explicitly rather than attributing performance gaps solely to catalog size.

The ultimate objective of toolkit engineering is an active catalog whose contracts align with workload demands while keeping execution costs and failure modes transparent. Static staging, on-demand selection, task-level abstractions, and expressive command runners represent trade-offs to evaluate against these cost and reliability metrics. The same engineering principles apply when an agent interacts with a graphical user interface instead of a programmatic API: mouse clicks, keyboard events, and visual screen parsers impose their own granularity challenges, prefill budgets, and containment boundaries.

## Visual Actuation and Computer Use {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-visual-actuation}

Consider the staging-container restart scenario when an administrative web dashboard provides no programmatic API. A **computer-use tool**\index{Computer-use tool!definition} bridges this interface gap by rendering visual screenshots to the model and translating model-generated targets into synthetic mouse clicks, keystrokes, or scrolling gestures—the low-level input space pioneered in early web-agent research [@shi2017world]. Operating on raw pixels does not relax system invariants. While the model proposes an interaction based on an observed frame, the execution runtime retains responsibility for validating arguments, enforcing authorization, dispatching OS events, and interpreting observations. A coordinate within display boundaries merely confirms that an event can reach the window manager, offering no assurance about the state mutation that the event will trigger.

### An action against a changing surface {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-changing-surface}

Suppose an agent session possesses authorization to restart the staging container `srv-stage-04`, but security policies strictly forbid modifying production workloads. The agent observes a confirmation modal that identifies the staging container and renders a clickable Restart button. Controlling this workflow requires the same rigorous interface contract used for structured tool calls, adapted for spatial and temporal dynamism.

When the runtime captures an observation, it records the application and window identifier, a unique capture identifier, an observation timestamp, and the exact geometric frame presented to the model. If the runtime downsamples, pads, or crops the image before model ingestion, it must retain the crop offsets and scaling factors needed to project a proposed coordinate back into the native display coordinate space. Raw screenshot pixels, application-relative window coordinates, and virtual desktop coordinates represent distinct spatial reference frames. The runtime adapter must validate all proposed points against the active viewport; silently clamping out-of-bounds coordinates to the nearest edge risks turning an invalid model hallucination into a destructive click on an unintended adjacent control.

Now suppose the model proposes clicking the Restart button based on that observation. Prior to event dispatch, the adapter must recheck the current application focus, active window state, and target dialog parameters using platform accessibility or windowing APIs. In a dynamic desktop environment, state changes rapidly. A background network event or concurrent operator action might bring a production container dialog into the foreground at those exact screen coordinates. In this scenario, valid spatial coordinates no longer justify executing the model's proposal. The runtime must detect the stale precondition, abort the pending dispatch, and request a fresh visual observation. While benign updates such as a ticking taskbar clock do not invalidate a target, any modification to a resource identifier, modal overlay, or button layout alters the operational effect.

Once the staging dialog is re-verified, the policy engine must evaluate the session grant against the intended container restart rather than checking a generic permission to emit mouse clicks. If the interface cannot establish which backend operation the click will execute with the confidence required by the security policy, the runtime must block dispatch and escalate the decision to an authorized operator. Otherwise, the adapter dispatches the bounded input event and records its immediate outcome. Structured endpoints enforce resource identity and action preconditions directly at the server interface, providing a robust execution boundary. By contrast, visual actuation cannot achieve atomic execution: capturing a fresh screenshot reduces staleness, but it cannot prevent a concurrent state change from slipping between the observation capture and the event dispatch.

After dispatching the input event, the subsequent observation must verify operational progress rather than mere input delivery. A disappearing confirmation modal might indicate that the server accepted the restart command, but it might also mean that a network timeout dismissed the dialog without action. The runtime must gather corroborating evidence of the restart, either by inspecting a refreshed dashboard status indicator or by issuing an authorized read-only status query. If the click produces no visible change and the dashboard continues displaying the previous state, the requested operation might still be processing asynchronously. Under these conditions, the execution yields an uncertain outcome (definition \ref{dfn-uncertain-outcome}), which the runtime must resolve through the idempotency and reconciliation protocols detailed in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency rather than by repeatedly firing redundant clicks.

### Visual observation budgets {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-visual-budgets}

Visual observations require the same rigorous resource accounting as textual tool payloads. Vision encoders partition input images into fixed-size grid patches, converting high-resolution screenshots into thousands of visual tokens. Because visual token consumption directly inflates inference latency and per-turn billing, systems engineers must monitor both the raw byte representation submitted to the model and its resulting token allocation.

Naively compressing visual inputs introduces sharp engineering trade-offs. Downscaling an entire screen capture reduces token consumption, but blurs fine visual details such as container names, port numbers, or warning banners until they become unreadable. Conversely, tightly cropping the image preserves full pixel resolution around a candidate button, but strips away peripheral context, concealing modal warning banners or active window titles that are essential for correct interpretation.

A resilient architecture balances these demands through hierarchical visual sampling: capturing a low-resolution full-screen overview to establish window layout and focus, paired with an on-demand, high-resolution crop around the target interaction zone. Each visual artifact must retain its parent observation identifier and affine coordinate mapping so the runtime can translate local crop coordinates back to native display space. Similarly, transmitting visual diffs of modified screen regions reduces payload size during iterative tasks, provided the diff retains sufficient surrounding landmark geometry for the vision model to orient itself. Because large language model inference engines rely on exact prefix matching for KV-cache reuse, altering a visual frame across turns invalidates cached prefixes for all subsequent tokens. A well-designed observation budget delivers the minimal visual evidence necessary to authorize and execute the next operational decision while keeping token consumption bounded.

::: {#chk-07-visual-contract .callout-checkpoint title="A click is still a tool call"}

A dashboard changes after the model observes a staging restart dialog. The adapter can capture the display and send a click, but cannot atomically bind that click to the displayed resource.

- [ ] **Target identity**: Which changes require rejecting the old proposal, and why is a coordinate-range check insufficient?
- [ ] **Observation geometry**: What information must accompany a resized crop so a proposed point can be mapped to the intended surface?
- [ ] **Authority and freshness**: What does a new screenshot establish, and which action-time uncertainty remains before dispatch?
- [ ] **Effect evidence**: If the click times out and the old status remains visible, why is another click not automatically justified? What evidence would support the intended restart without claiming the whole task is complete?

:::
## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-fallacies}

The tool boundary fails when evidence about one stage is treated as a guarantee about another. These misconceptions recur across structured, terminal, and visual interfaces.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A schema-valid call is safe to execute.*
