Structural validity checks the shape of a request; the session's grant, the current domain preconditions, and resource limits are separate checks (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-schemas). In the GitHub MCP leak (war story \ref{ws-07-github-mcp-2025}), every call the agent made was schema-valid and within its credential's reach. The call that exceeded the task's grants was the first private-repository read, and no check compared it with the task.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating a timeout as permission to retry.*

A timeout records missing knowledge, not a failure. Under the blind-retry model of notebook \ref{nbk-07-settlement-budget}, a per-call duplicate probability of `{python} SettlementBudget.duplicate_str` becomes about `{python} SettlementBudget.duplicates_per_day_str` duplicate effects a day across `{python} SettlementBudget.calls_per_day_str` mutating calls. Retry only on safe operation semantics, an endpoint that honors the operation ID, or reconciliation evidence (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency); otherwise record the effect as unresolved.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A zero exit status establishes task completion.*

Exit status is the invoked program's convention. A runner that discovers zero tests, a script without `pipefail`, and a client that prints its error and exits normally all return zero (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-observation-parsing). The `r18` reproducer pass supports one exercised connection-pool case; acceptance follows the task's evidence standard (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}).
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Shrinking an observation without recording what was dropped.*

Truncation itself is unavoidable, since the illustrative log in notebook \ref{nbk-07-observation-budget} is `{python} ObservationBudget.raw_windows_mult_str` the entire context window. The mistake is losing the record of omission. A head-only policy applied to @lst-vol3-head-truncation keeps the banner and passing tests and drops the one panic that explains the failure. The head, notice, and tail of @eq-vol3-observation-byte-budget keep it within the same byte budget, and an inspection handle recovers the middle on request.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *Staging every registered tool is harmless because each descriptor is short.*

Descriptors add up, and they recur on every call. In notebook \ref{nbk-07-memory-footprint-and-prefill-latency}, a `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.registered_tools_str`-tool catalog occupies `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.static_tokens_str` tokens of each request, while the `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.selected_tools_str` tools a step needs, with selection overhead, use `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.selected_total_str`. Over a trajectory that difference is paid once per turn, in capacity taken from task evidence (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-toolkit-design).
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Letting the model poll a long-running job.*

Each "still running" answer is a full model call. In notebook \ref{nbk-07-token-cost-and-inference-overhead}, a `{python} PollingBudget.job_s_str` job checked every `{python} PollingBudget.interval_s_str` costs `{python} PollingBudget.pending_calls_str` extra model calls and `{python} PollingBudget.extra_cost_str` in tokens that change no decision. Runtime polling or a completion notification detects the change without inference and wakes the model only when the result can alter the next action (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-resumption).
:::
## Summary {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-summary}

Every runtime mechanism in this chapter enforces a single operational discipline: an agent may base its next decision only on what returning evidence directly confirms. A schema validates the syntactic shape of a request, an authorization grant restricts its permissible targets, an endpoint check enforces execution preconditions and timing, and an observation reports what the tool actually measured. None of these mechanisms assumes that a proposed operation successfully altered external state, nor does a completed execution guarantee that the broader task has succeeded. When evidence is missing—as occurred during the timed-out staging restart—the runtime must record the evidentiary gap explicitly rather than interpolating an assumed outcome.

@Tbl-vol3-tool-calling-key-equations summarizes the quantitative relations governing dispatch concurrency, retry safety, and observation overhead across the tool boundary, where $q_{\text{req}}$ and $q_{\text{rep}}$ denote independent request- and reply-loss probabilities, $R_i$ and $W_i$ represent the declared read and write footprints of call $i$, and an asynchronous job of duration $T_{\text{job}}$ polled at intervals of $\Delta t$ incurs per-token input and output prices $c_{\text{in}}$ and $c_{\text{out}}$.

| Equation                                                                                                                                 | What it bounds or decides                                                                                                                          | Where derived                           |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------|
| $W_i \cap (R_j \cup W_j) = \emptyset$ and $W_j \cap R_i = \emptyset$                                                                     | Whether two batched calls may run concurrently; valid only for trustworthy footprints                                                              | @sec-vol3-tool-calling-unix-analogy     |
| $N_{\text{host}} \times N_{\text{tool}}$ adapters vs. $N_{\text{host}} + N_{\text{tool}}$                                                | Integration work for $N_{\text{host}}$ hosts and $N_{\text{tool}}$ tool services, with and without a shared protocol                               | @sec-vol3-tool-calling-mcp              |
| $f(f(s)) = f(s)$                                                                                                                         | Whether a timed-out operation may be repeated without settlement, for the named state                                                              | @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency      |
| $p_{\text{timeout}} = 1-(1-q_{\text{req}})(1-q_{\text{rep}})$; $p_{\text{dup}} = (1-q_{\text{req}})\,q_{\text{rep}}\,(1-q_{\text{req}})$ | Timeout rate and duplicate-effect rate under one blind retry; duplicates track reply loss                                                          | @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency      |
| $\mathbb{T}_\theta = \langle \text{actuate}(\theta),\ \text{probe}(\theta, s_0),\ \text{compensate}(\theta) \rangle$                     | What a mutating tool without endpoint deduplication must ship so a timeout can be reconciled                                                       | @eq-vol3-legacy-tool-contract           |
| $M_{\text{obs},\max} = M_{\text{head}} + M_{\text{notice}} + M_{\text{tail}}$                                                            | Fixed capture memory and staged size for a log of any length, and which diagnostic region survives                                                 | @eq-vol3-observation-byte-budget        |
| $S_{\text{obs}} \cdot H_{\text{rem}}$ carried input tokens                                                                               | Later input cost of one staged observation of $S_{\text{obs}}$ tokens selected for $H_{\text{rem}}$ further calls                                  | @sec-vol3-tool-calling-streaming        |
| $N_{\text{poll}} = \lceil T_{\text{job}}/\Delta t \rceil - 1$, costing $N_{\text{poll}}(S\,c_{\text{in}} + K\,c_{\text{out}})$           | Inference spent on model-directed status checks that runtime detection avoids                                                                      | @sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-resumption |
| $(n_{\text{reg}} - n_{\text{sel}})\,S_{\text{desc}} > S_{\text{sel}}$                                                                    | When selecting $n_{\text{sel}}$ of $n_{\text{reg}}$ descriptors of $S_{\text{desc}}$ tokens pays for $S_{\text{sel}}$ tokens of selection overhead | @sec-vol3-tool-calling-toolkit-design   |

: **Key equations of the tool boundary**: Each relation holds only under the assumptions stated where it is derived, such as independent message loss, a fixed selected payload, or declared footprints that omit no shared state. {#tbl-vol3-tool-calling-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[40,38,22]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="A tool call includes its returning evidence"}

* **A call ends at its observation, not its dispatch**: The runtime matches each returning result to its corresponding invocation, recording whether the proposal was rejected, dispatched, completed, or left in an indeterminate state. Subsequent planning must reason strictly from this confirmed disposition rather than assuming an action succeeded simply because the host dispatched it.
* **Schemas shape requests; enforcement governs effects**: Type signatures and parameter descriptions guide the model to structure valid calls, but authorization grants, resource quotas, and precondition checks govern actual execution. Any mutation that depends on an unchanged target resource must verify preconditions atomically alongside the write, rather than relying on stale observations from an earlier read.
* **Discovery does not confer permission**: Exposing a tool interface in the context window reveals structural syntax, but connectivity and schema compliance never imply authorization. The host runtime must validate every invocation against task-scoped grants—including read-only queries—while the remote endpoint enforces its own perimeter independently.
* **An unknown effect forbids blind repetition**: Because a timed-out attempt may have committed before network acknowledgment was lost, duplicate side effects track reply loss rather than request loss. The runtime may retry an unacknowledged invocation only under provably idempotent semantics, an endpoint deduplication contract, or explicit probe reconciliation. Otherwise, it must preserve the operation as an unresolved effect.
* **Truncation must disclose what it dropped**: Buffer limits and model context windows constrain distinct physical resources, yet both force data omission. An observation payload that incorporates execution status, provenance metadata, and a measured omission counter preserves diagnostic integrity, whereas silent head truncation often discards the terminal error or stack trace needed to diagnose a fault.
* **Acknowledgment is not completion**: Long-running jobs require durable handles, scoped inspection, authorized input channels, and unambiguous cancellation outcomes. Event-driven runtime detection re-awakens the model only when a state change can alter the next action, preventing empty polling loops that burn inference budgets on uninformative checks.
* **No toolkit size is universally optimal**: Catalog staging and API granularity navigate a fundamental trade-off among context overhead, selection accuracy, expressiveness, and security boundaries, while visual interfaces introduce freshness and target-geometry constraints. System designers must evaluate a toolkit by its total cost per accepted task and the precision of the authority it leaves bounded.

:::

The typed action contract (principle \ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}) cleanly separates an interpretable proposal emitted by the model from the authorization required to execute it. When network drops or timeouts leave an outcome ambiguous, settlement before retry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement})\index{Principle!settlement before retry} extends that discipline to prevent silent state corruption: the runtime must either establish that repeating the call is safe or record an unresolved effect. Crucially, a tool's completion report confirms only that an operation finished, not that the overall task succeeded. Final acceptance always demands invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}), verifying that the system's operational requirements hold in reality before declaring success.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-history}

The tool execution boundary is the modern incarnation of a problem operating systems encountered half a century ago: an untrusted program requests an operation that the system cannot permit it to perform directly. In a 1972 computer security planning study for the U.S. Air Force, Anderson introduced the concept of the reference monitor, establishing three non-negotiable requirements for access control: the monitor must be tamper-proof, always invoked, and small enough to be subjected to rigorous analysis and verification [@anderson1972computer]. Saltzer and Schroeder synthesized these insights into foundational design principles—most notably complete mediation, least privilege, and economy of mechanism—which dictate that every access path must be validated and that protection mechanisms should remain minimal and transparent [@saltzer1975]. Dennis and Van Horn had earlier introduced capability-based addressing, wherein possession of an unforgeable token directly conveys the authority to act [@dennis1966], while Lampson formalized access policies into a canonical matrix defining the rights held by subjects over system objects [@lampson1974protection]. Hardy's 1988 analysis of the confused deputy problem revealed the hazards of ambient authority, showing what goes wrong when a privileged service executes operations on behalf of an unprivileged client without checking the client's authority [@hardy1988confused]. In agent runtimes, this exact vulnerability manifests whenever a model holding private credentials executes operations triggered by untrusted user prompts or retrieved external content.

A second historical lineage governs operations that cross network boundaries. Birrell and Nelson designed the Remote Procedure Call (RPC) to make remote invocations feel as natural as local function calls, but they documented the fundamental tension of distributed execution: during network partitions or server crashes, a caller cannot know whether a request succeeded, failed, or stalled midway through execution [@birrell1984rpc]. In the same year, Saltzer, Reed, and Clark articulated the end-to-end argument, demonstrating that reliability and correctness cannot be guaranteed solely by intermediate communication layers and must ultimately be validated by the endpoints themselves [@saltzer1984endtoend]. Distributed systems researchers developed several robust patterns to handle this inherent ambiguity. Kung and Robinson introduced optimistic concurrency control, allowing transactions to proceed without heavy upfront locking and validating serializability before commit [@kung1981optimistic]. For distributed operations that cannot be rolled back atomically, Garcia-Molina and Salem formulated sagas, coordinating sequences of local transactions coupled with compensating actions to undo partially completed work [@garciamolina1987sagas]. Gray and Cheriton introduced leases, using time-bounded grants to manage shared resources without requiring indefinite locks [@gray1989leases]. Finally, Helland made the practical case that reliable distributed systems must push retry safety into the receiver by enforcing endpoint idempotence [@helland2012idempotence]—a requirement that directly informs how tool runtimes deduplicate requests and handle agent retries.

Language models converged on tool execution from the opposite direction, evolving from passive sequence predictors into interactive system callers. Early modular architectures routed model queries to external calculators, symbolic solvers, and database interfaces [@karpas2022mrkl]. @yao2023react established the ReAct paradigm, demonstrating that interleaving explicit reasoning traces with concrete actions and environment feedback dramatically improves multi-step problem solving. @schick2023toolformer showed with Toolformer that models could learn in a self-supervised manner to propose external API calls spontaneously, complete with appropriate arguments, during standard text generation. As the scope of external tools expanded, retrieval-augmented tool selection helped eliminate hallucinated function signatures by fetching accurate documentation on demand [@patil2023gorilla], while large-scale instruction tuning exposed models to thousands of diverse, real-world REST APIs [@qin2024toolllm]. Interacting with external environments also has roots in web agents that manipulate user interfaces through simulated keyboard and mouse events [@shi2017world]. However, designing interfaces specifically tailored to language models proved even more effective: @yang2024sweagent demonstrated with SWE-agent that structuring the agent-computer interface around model-friendly commands—such as concise file viewers with line numbers and restricted editing primitives—substantially lifted task success on complex software engineering benchmarks. To manage the proliferation of heterogeneous tools, open specifications like the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardized the boundary between host runtimes and external tool servers [@mcp2025specification]. Yet as tool calling gained ubiquity, it exposed a unique vulnerability: because an agent interprets untrusted external text within the same context window that guides its decisions, adversarial inputs can steer the model into executing unintended tool invocations [@greshake2023not]. Because the language model is an untrusted caller that can be influenced by malicious prompts, the enclosing systems runtime must enforce complete mediation, least privilege, and idempotence on every operation.

For further reading:

- Saltzer and Schroeder, "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems" [@saltzer1975]. The canonical catalog of security principles for computer systems. Read through the lens of agent execution, principles like complete mediation, least privilege, and economy of mechanism serve as a direct checklist for designing secure tool boundaries.
- Birrell and Nelson, "Implementing Remote Procedure Calls" [@birrell1984rpc]. The foundational paper on RPC and the clearest exposition of distributed failure semantics. It establishes why a caller can never be completely certain whether an unacknowledged remote call executed, providing the theoretical basis for retry budgets and timeout policies.
- Hardy, "The Confused Deputy" [@hardy1988confused]. A concise, three-page paper that identifies how an entity with broad ambient authority becomes an unwitting tool for attackers. It represents required reading for understanding why language agents must never carry ambient credentials across security domains.
- Helland, "Idempotence Is Not a Medical Condition" [@helland2012idempotence]. A practical guide to designing distributed systems that survive retries by pushing deduplication and idempotence keys into receiver interfaces, directly applicable to tool runtime dispatch.
- Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design* [@ousterhout2018philosophy]. A masterclass on interface design and deep modules. The book's criteria for module depth and interface complexity provide concrete guidance for sizing tool APIs so models can invoke them effectively without leaking implementation details.
- Yang et al., "SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering" [@yang2024sweagent]. An empirical demonstration that designing clean, model-oriented tool interfaces is just as vital to agent performance as scaling the underlying language model.

## Exercises {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-exercises}

All quantities below are hypothetical problem givens, chosen to be round, and describe no particular provider, protocol version, or deployment. Assume message losses are independent unless a problem says otherwise.

**1. Blind retry at fleet volume (Basic).** A tool fleet issues 120,000 mutating calls a day to an endpoint with no deduplication. Each request is lost with probability 1 percent and each reply with probability 3 percent; lost messages never arrive later, and every timeout triggers exactly one retry.

(a) Compute the per-call timeout probability, the per-call duplicate-effect probability, and the expected duplicates per day.
(b) A network team offers two upgrades: halve reply loss, or halve request loss. Compute the daily duplicates under each and explain why one of them slightly *increases* duplicates.
(c) Name the change that removes the duplicate path rather than shrinking it, and state what the endpoint must bind the identifier to for that change to hold.

**2. Sizing the tail (Basic).** An adapter stages test logs with a head-and-tail policy under $M_{\text{obs},\max} = 16{,}384$ bytes, with $M_{\text{notice}} = 256$ bytes and $M_{\text{head}} = 4{,}096$ bytes. A failing run writes 9,000,000 bytes in total. Its only diagnostic is a 2,400-byte panic block, followed by 11,000 bytes of teardown output and a 600-byte final summary.

(a) Compute $M_{\text{tail}}$ and determine whether the whole panic block reaches the model.
(b) Keeping $M_{\text{obs},\max}$ and $M_{\text{notice}}$ fixed, find the largest $M_{\text{head}}$ that keeps the entire panic block in the tail. How many bytes does the omission notice report in either configuration?
(c) The same runner sometimes prints the panic before 200,000 bytes of teardown output. Explain why no split of this $M_{\text{obs},\max}$ fixes that case, and name the mechanism from @sec-vol3-tool-calling-streaming that does.

**3. When catalog selection pays (Basic).** A repair harness registers 80 tools, each contributing 420 tokens to the final serialized request. On-demand staging exposes 8 of them plus 900 tokens of selection interface and metadata, and the runtime selects without an extra model call. A trajectory makes 40 model calls, and uncached input costs \$3 per million tokens.

(a) Compute the catalog input of one call under each layout, the capacity released per call, and the break-even number of unused descriptors.
(b) Compute the tokens and uncached dollars released over the trajectory.
(c) In one trajectory out of five, a needed tool was not staged and the agent spends one extra model call of 30,000 input tokens rediscovering it. Does selection still pay? State the condition under which the comparison would flip.
(d) The 80 descriptors come from three interoperable tool servers discovered at session start. One of them advertises `delete_branch` with a description stating that it is approved for all repositories, and the task's grants do not include branch deletion. Does staging or omitting that descriptor change what the agent may do? Name the check that governs the call if the model proposes it anyway, where each part of that check runs, and what the returned observation should report.

**4. The price of asking whether a job finished (Intermediate).** A repair agent's test suite completes after 1,500 s. Under model-directed polling, the model checks every 30 s, starting one interval after dispatch, with each status call reading a 48,000-token selected input and generating 60 tokens. The cache covers 90 percent of that input. Hypothetical prices per million tokens are \$3 uncached input, \$0.30 cached input, and \$15 output. The fleet runs 2,000 such jobs a day.

(a) Compute the pending-status calls per job, the incremental cost per job, and the daily fleet cost of polling.
(b) Product management caps model-directed polling at \$0.10 per job. Find the minimum poll interval that meets the cap, and the worst-case delay between completion and detection at that interval for a job whose completion time is not known in advance.
(c) Runtime polling every 10 s costs no inference. Compare its worst-case detection delay and token cost with the answer to (b), then choose a design to ship and state what model-directed inspection remains useful for.

**5. Retrying a refund (Intermediate; second lighthouse).** The support agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}) issues refunds through a payment endpoint that offers no deduplication contract. It sends 40,000 refund calls a day, each averaging \$60. Requests are lost with probability 0.5 percent and replies with probability 1.5 percent. The alternative to blind retry is an authorized reconciliation probe written before dispatch (@eq-vol3-legacy-tool-contract), which adds 4 s to the customer's wait on every timed-out call.

(a) Under one blind retry per timeout, compute the expected duplicate refunds per day and their dollar exposure.
(b) Under the probe policy, compute the fraction of sessions that incur the extra wait and the total added customer wait per day.
(c) For the repair agent a duplicated test run costs tokens; here the binding constraint is response latency, yet the answer still favors settlement. Justify that decision numerically, and explain why a refund's operation ID must not be a hash of the customer and amount.

**6. Carry, drop, or re-read (Intermediate).** A repair agent stages a 6,000-token test observation that stays in context for its remaining 45 model calls. Uncached input costs \$3 per million tokens. An alternative policy keeps the observation for the 5 calls in which it informs a decision, then replaces it with a 300-token summary carrying an inspection handle for the rest of the trajectory. Each later re-read through the handle costs one extra model call with 40,000 input tokens and returns a 2,000-token slice that stays in context for 5 calls.

(a) Compute the carried input tokens and uncached cost of keeping the observation, and the same for dropping it with no re-reads.
(b) Find the number of re-reads at which dropping stops being cheaper.
(c) Tokens are not the only cost of a re-read. Identify one latency cost and one evidence risk the ledger in (a) omits, and state which of them would change the policy for a log whose failure sits in the omitted middle.

**7. Scheduling a batch by footprint (Intermediate).** A response proposes five calls for the connection-pool repair, listed with durations and declared footprints. `read_source(pool.py)` takes 2 s and reads `pool.py`. `read_source(config.py)` takes 2 s and reads `config.py`. `apply_patch(pool.py)` takes 1 s, reads and writes `pool.py`, and uses the version returned by the first read. `run_tests` takes 30 s, reads `pool.py`, `config.py`, and `tests/`, and writes `.cache`. `lint(pool.py)` takes 5 s, reads `pool.py`, and writes `.cache`. The workflow requires tests and lint to see the patched file.

(a) Apply the noninterference condition to find which pairs may overlap, then give the shortest schedule and its makespan. Compare with fully serial dispatch.
(b) Changing the linter to write `.lintcache` instead is a one-line configuration change. Compute the new makespan.
(c) The model proposes replacing `lint` and `run_tests` with one `bash -c "make check"` call that runs both in sequence for 35 s and whose footprint is undeclared. What must the runtime do with it, and what does that cost in makespan relative to (b)?
(d) Between the read of `pool.py` and `apply_patch`, a teammate commits a change to the same file. The patch arguments still pass schema validation. State which descriptor field and which endpoint operation reject the stale patch, why a separate version check before the write is insufficient, and what the rejection returned to the model should contain.

**8. Retention windows and delayed attempts (Advanced).** A runtime retries a mutating call against an endpoint that deduplicates by operation ID. Each attempt waits a 10 s timeout, then backs off 1, 2, 4, and 8 s before attempts two through five. The network can delay a request by up to 120 s before delivery. The endpoint retains operation IDs for 60 s after first receipt.

(a) Compute the send time of each attempt and the retention window needed so that no delivered attempt of this operation can execute a second time.
(b) The endpoint's retention is fixed at 60 s. Show that no schedule containing even one retry closes the gap, then redesign the contract so the endpoint rejects any request issued more than 45 s earlier. Assuming clocks agree within 2 s, which attempts may the runtime still send?
(c) Critique the redesign. What new failure mode does request expiry introduce, what outcome must the runtime record when every permitted attempt times out, and which settlement mechanism from @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency takes over?

**9. One shell or twelve tools (Advanced; second lighthouse).** A team proposes giving the remediation agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}) a single `run_shell` tool with a 500-token descriptor in place of 12 structured tools of 350 tokens each, citing fewer selection errors. A trajectory makes 30 model calls at \$3 per million uncached input tokens. With structured tools, an attempt costs \$1.20, is accepted with probability 0.80, and causes an unconfined production change with probability 0.001; with the shell those figures are an attempt cost reduced by the descriptor savings, acceptance probability 0.78, and unconfined-change probability 0.004. Each unconfined change costs \$2,000 to detect and repair.

(a) Compute the per-trajectory descriptor savings and $C_{\text{eff}} = \mathbb{E}[C_{\text{attempt}}]/p_{\text{acc}}$ for each design, first from token costs alone and then including expected change losses in the attempt cost.
(b) Find the unconfined-change probability the shell design would need to match the structured design's $C_{\text{eff}}$.
(c) Critique the team's evaluation metric, and propose a toolkit that keeps most of the descriptor savings without the loss. Say which mechanism bounds the shell's reach and which staging policy recovers context capacity.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From tool interfaces to execution isolation"}

A well-specified, authorized tool can still execute faulty or untrusted code. Its descriptor does not limit which files that implementation can reach, which external services it can contact, or how many resources it can consume. @Sec-vol3-sandboxes develops the execution envelope that enforces those limits beneath the running code, extending the tool contract from permitted requests to contained execution.

:::
